div.p: Wattrg.
THE BATTLE OF THE BIRDS.

• AN ApoLocum BY HAMILTON AIDE. A discussion among British birds once arose, As to where they should praise the Almighty; The reverend faction of Rooks were the foes Of the Swallows, whose tenets wen—flighty. These wanderers lax from the South cried, "Rejoice! No matter the soil or the tree, On which one alighteth to lift up his voice To the Lord of the land and the sea!" "Not so," cawed the Rooks, with a vehemence fit Opposition to drown, or o'erwhelm ; "For worship, in one place alone must all sit, 'Neath the high Gothic arch of the elm. The Cardinal, Parrot, or such foreign bird, 'Neath the palm's rounded dome he may perch; But we, who are quite set apart from the herd, Should abjure pagan forms for a church. That impudent Wren has selected a larch, Whose boughs form a cupola quite; [arch, We must carry down twigs from our elm's Gothic To make it an orthodox site" Then a great storm arose, while the advocates fought, The Geese cackled round as of old; The Magpies repeated the words they were taught, The Gulls swallowed all they were told. The Owls hooted round their discordant assent To the dreariest doctrine. The Dove Coo'd in vain, 'mid the tumult, and did not resent That none heard her message of love. 'DU the Lark, soaring no to the blue summer sky, ' Rained down her notes o'er the crowd; E'en the Nightinc,,ale's singing was hushed by the high Small voice that was heard from the cloud. "I am nighest to heaven, and •up here, my friends, Yonr squabbles appear very small; Every spot whence the voice of true worship ascends Is blest by the Maker of all. Sing out in the wild wood, ye Mavis and Merle! Ye Ptarmigans, cry o'er the moor! Caw, ye reverend Rooks, round the elms of the earl! Robins, pipe round the homes of the poor! The Master who 'once each a different tone, And a plumage diverse as our birth, Never meant that one form of a tree or a stone Should be hallowed alone upon earth. [roof, Let the Rook have his lancet-shaped aisle and groined His dome of rich foliage the Wren; Then shall Birds, in their harmony, carry reproof To the turbulent Children of Men." —" Good Words" for March.

div.p: Tarittits.

_ Grace has very curly hair, and It was a great trial to her to have it combed. One day during this process she was crying and making a greater disturbance than usual, when the mother said: "What will the neighbours say when they hear you making such a noise ?" Pausing amid her weeping, she said, in broken tones: "They'll say. 'Why don't that woman spank that child?" Planche writes—My old fellow-traveller in Germany: himself an Irishman, being on the box of an Irish mail coach oda very cold day, and observing the driver en- veloping his neck in the voluminous folds of an ample, "comforter," remarked, "You seem to be taking very good care of yourself, my friend?" "Oh, to be sure I am, sir, answered the driver; "what's all the world to a man when his wife's a widdy ?" Charles Kemble told the story of how, one day, he was followed up Sackville-street, Dublin, by two beggar- women, between whom the following dialogue passed, evidently with a view to his edification :—" Och, but he's ap illigant man, is Misther Charles Kemble !" "An'. 'deed, so was his brudher. Misther John, thin—a moighty foine man! and to see his demanour, puttin' his hand in his pocket and givin' me sixpence, bate all the viorld !" It is told of the late Dr. Winter Hamilton, of Brighton, that one day he went into the town to buy a fish. The fish-monger was a female member of the Society of Friends. Having made his purchase, he requested her to send it to his house. "What is thy address?" asked she. lie replied: "Direct it to the Rev. W. Hamilton, at such a place." She hesitated a little, and then, taking a card and a pen and ink, she handed them to him and said: "Perhaps thou wilt reverence thyself." Manners are of more importance than laws. Upon them, in a great measure, the laws depend. The law touches us but here and there, now and then. Manners are what vex and soothe, corrupt or purify, exalt or debase, barbarise or refine us, by a constant, steady. uniform, insensible operation, like that of the air we breathe in. They give their whole form and colour to' our lives. according to their quality, they aid morals; I they supply them or they totally destroy them. As to eondersation—Bishop Thirlwall was deaf. Although deafness hiterfered with his enjoyment of con- versation, he thought little of if loss. Once when he was walking in the road, a friend veho knew perfectly well the bishop's infirmity, remarked, "It's Wee, my lord bishop." "Eh ?" said the bishop. "It's wet, my lofel." "Eh ?" repeated the bishop. The observation had to be made several times before the bishop could catch its meaning. "Strange how little one loses by being deaf !" he exclaimed. An acquaintance of mine (says Planche) who frequently visited Ireland, and generally stopped and dined at the same hotel in Dublin, on his arrival one day, perceived a paper wafered on the looking-glass in the coffee-room with the following written notice :—" Strangers are par- ticularly requested not to give any money to the waiters, as attendance is charged for in the bill." The man who bad waited on him at dinner, seeing him reading this nctiee, said, "Oh, Misther —, sure that don't concern youTh any whlt. Your honour was niver made a stranger of in this house." A Bridgeport eapee !lays that a detective of that city; teeleeel leived the following letter :—`• Will you oblige I me by going to some picture gallery and set for my pic- tures. I will pay you. My children and relations are bothering me to have one took, as I am groesin' old, and as I am buzzy gitting in crops I can't spair time to come down. I hear you have dizgizes so you can de as well as me. Have on red side whiskers and good clothes. Make the picture good lookine and when you laff show your teeth, as I have a bran new set of false ones. lam 48 years old, and a widower." Some years ago a young Scotchman tried his luck at the Monte Carlo gambling tables) and eves fortunate enough to win a very large sum—between £20,000 and £30,000. On returning to his hotel he handed the money to his valet—a tried old family servant—and on the following morning was dumbfounded to learn that the valet had disappeared. Several days passed without any tidings of the runaway, but at length a telegram arrived from the valet in Scotland, announcing that he had lost no time in hurrying home to place the money in the hands of the young man's father, which he regarded as a safer place of deposit than a Monte Carlo hoteL A young student, walking with another round the Calton-hill at Edinburgh, began to expatiate on the matchless beauty and infinite variety of the views which were to be obtained from that site; and he at length confessed that, inspired by the admirable prospect of the coast of Fife, on the epposite side of the Firth of Forth, he had commenced, a poem in its praise; but he had somehow, failed to get beyond the first line— Again we see. upon the northern shore— Why, man," answered his companion, "I think it would be no difficult matter to make that a couplet. Let me see— Klnghorn still standing where it stood before." When / was in Italy (says Mark Boyd) a quarter of a century back, it used to be alleged that, pay an Italian piestboy as liberally as you liked, he still would ask you for a " buono mano." The Irish Dublin carman is said to belong to the Italian school in this respect. The peculiarity came on the tapis at a dinner party at Morri- son's Hotel in Dublin, when one of the party present defended Paddy from what he considered an unjust imputation; and in support of his opinion, offered to bet his friends £lO that he would drive from their hotel to the Rotunda, at the top of Sackville-street, and back without any such importunity, one of the party to accompany him, as a guarantee that nothing ez curia was said to Paddy en route. Accordingly, an outside car was sent for, and started for the Rotunda, the rest of the party awaiting its return outside the hoteL Paddy set down his two passengers, and was presenfed wit') three half-crowns, being more than three times his fare. He turned them over in his hand, and then said, " Och, yet honour, can't you make it.into the nate half-sovereign?" A YORKSHIRE SUPERS.TITION.—In Yorkshire, the Kirk- I Grim is usually a huge black dog with eyes like saucers,' and is called a padfoot. It generally frequents the church lanes; and he who sees it knows that he must di- within the year. And now—to somewhat relieve this ghastly subject—we may tell an odd incident con- nneted with it, to which the writer contributed some- thing. On a stormy night in November, be was out w ith a big umbrella over his head, that had a handle of NO-lite bone. A sudden gust—and the umbrella was whisked out of his hand, and carried away into the in- mete darkness and mist of rain. The same night a friend of his was walking down a . very lonely church line, between hedges slid fields, without a house near. In the loneliest, most haunted portion of the lane, his feet and his pulsation and breath were suddenly arrested ly the sight of a great black creature, occupying the middle of the way, shaking itself impatiently, moving forward, and then bounding on one side, then running to the other. No saucer eyes, it is true, were visible, but it had a white nose that, to the horrified traveller, asemed lit with a supernatural phosphoric radiance. AT A FRENCH DINNER.—An old veteran of the New York press, George Canfield, used to tell of a comical adventure which befell him in Paris. George had laboured long and industriously at the ship-news desk. He resided in the " Burg " as they used to call the eastern district of Brooklyn, and had worked himself up from the ease, where he "set the ships," until he became editor-in-chief of the department. He knew enough of French to glean the exchanges for French vessels and the French marine ports and other terms, hut otherwise his knowledge of the language was greatly restricted. He had saved a good deal of money, and when, at length, he was given a generous holiday, he decided to spend it in Paris. His first, dinner in France was eaten at one of the big hotels in the Capital. His wife was with him. They consulted the bill of fare and I George pointed with his finger to the first item. The waiter bowed, went off and soon returned with a copious supply of soup for two. It was palatable, and George did full justice to it. Consulting the bill of fare once more, he pointed to the second item, somewhat to the surprise of the garcon. But he nodded his head emphatically and ejaculated " oui " two or three times. The conquered waiter brought him two more plates of soup. George had to pretend now that he was very fond of soap, so he ate it with great relish, although , it had a very filling effect. When it was all disposed of he took up the bill, and firmly convinced that he would surely strike something solid by going down two or three items on the list, he put his finger on the fourth or fifth line and pantomimed his desire to be served with what it represented. The waiter gave a little start, but rushed off to obey and brought back yet two more dishes of soup. George accepted his fate with a calm dignity. He wasn't going to let the waiter know thatll() wasn't getting just what he wanted, and he put himself outside the liquid with a good deal of effort and pretended gusto. "Well, Jennie," he said, as he took up the card once more, "I think we have had enough soup to get along without the roast. Suppose we skip down to the dessert." Bound ' to make no mistake this time he pointed to the last item. The waiter looked surprised. But George insisted. The polite garcon surrendered again, with a little shrug of the shoulders and brought the required article. "And whdt do you think it was?" asked George, when he told the story. "It was a bunch of toothpicks." AN EARTILLT Pees.ntse.—Does anybody weary for a "lodge in some vast wilderness?" That very undesira- ble residence is now a little difficult to be bad. The world is fast filling up, and railways, steamboats, and tour contractors are agencies most inimical to hermits of all degrees. Still there is a chance, and to a man weary of his: species I can entirely recommend Lord Howe Island. Out of the multiplicity of isles "amid the melan- choly main," it is puzzling on even a good atlas to pick the one dedicated to the hero of" the glorious Ist of June." Ships sail in and out of Sydney Harbour, yet few ever land at this tiny islet, discovered as far back as 1788 by Lieutenant Henry Ball, while on a voyage to Norfold Island from Port Jackson, in New South Wales. No land lies nearer it than Port Macquarie, 300 miles west, and Norfolk Island is nearlv double the distance i from this lonely Only ahoul: seven miles long and ' two or three in breadth at its greatest width, a vessel Might be alnint In the a icinity'of it without being aware of its situation, were it not for the high oceanic peak of Ball's Pyramid, which can be seen twelve or thirteen miles distant. But its own hills are even higher, Mount Gower being 2.800 feet and Mount Lidgbird some 400 feet lower. The soil is volcanic, but rich, and covered with a bounteous vegetation of palms, screw pines, and wild I figs, and a dense undergrowth of ferns, grasses, and the fairy-like orchids that twine from trunk to trunk. Wild pigs are the only bush animals, but goats are nearly as abundant as they were on that other island of romance whilom reputed to be the home of Robinson Crusoe, of York mariner. Fruit trees and culinary vegitables grow abundantly, and among the first features which strike the weather-beaten seamen who comes on this summer isle of Eden are the orange-groves, and the patches of water-melons, pomegranates, onions, potatoes, Indian eorn, pumpkins, and tobacco—all of which have been introduced. Vines grow well, and the banana ripens its great golden bunches of delicious fruit. Dogs yelp round the houses,. oxen plough the ittches of cultivated land, horses there are few, while the cat, which follows woman all over the world, is on Lord Howe Island kept in full occupation by the swarms of mice which have taken up their quarters in this secluded siding of the globe. There are swarms of ducks, pigeons, paroquets, magpies, doves, and mutton birds, valuable for their oil, though net par- ticularly toefthsome as food, while off the reefs fish of many kinds can be caught in abundance. No reptile, not even a lizard, exists on the island; and its woods are frequented by no animals more terrible than pigs and errant cats, who dine sumptuously on parrots and turtle doves every day of their vagabond lives. Even in that prosaic Admiralty paper from which we take these par- ticulars the land seems a paradise, and none the less paradisaical because it is a small one.—" Tly Countries of the World," February.

div.head: MR. CHAMBERLAIN AND MR.
div.p: MR. CHAMBERLAIN AND MR.
HOWES. (Elton THE "DAILY NEWS.")

Sir,—l notice a paragraph in your paper of to-day concerning Mr. Chamberlain- and myself. Will you allow me to point out that Mr. Chamberlain does not, in his reply. touch the question I raised in my lecture at Warrington. What I said was that at the last election Mr. Chamberlain and, others destir- ted Mr. Gladstone and threw in their lot with Lord Salisbury and the Tory party, and that we hare a I Tory Government in existence at the present time I because of the action of the seceding Liberals. The last general election turned more on the Land Pur- chase than the Home Ride Bill, and the Tories got a great number of votes by their misrepresentation of Mr. Gladstone's Land Purchase Scheme. Mr. Chamberlain gave the people to understand that Mr. Gladstone proposed to buy out the Irish land- lords at the English taxpayers expense, and with this cry, the Tories and seceding Liberals called the voters to the poll. On the 19th of August, 1886, Lord Salisbury made a speech in the House of Lords. He pointed out that the Tory Government had appointed a Commission. ..to inquire into the state of agriculture in Ireland, and he said: "But if it should come 3ut that the Land Courts have raade blunders and that there is that impossibility in any case of paying rent, I think it is not the landlords who should bear the loss. I think this would be one of the cases for the application of the principle of purchase by the State, and that the State, and not the landlords, must suffer for the errors of the past." Thus we, see Lord Salisbury advocating the very thing he had denounced dur- ing the election; and I asked at Warrington, what I ask again now, "has Mr: Chamberlain or any protested against other, leading Liberal dissentielA Lord Salisbury's change of front ;. or do they still intend to support him now that he is-in favour of the very thing they supported him in opposing ?" I do not ask what Mr. Ch'airiberlain' '-kf opinion is concerning the Irish land question at the present time; but what about this acrobatic feat performed by the man whom Mr. Chamberlain was instrumen- tal in returning to power ?—I am, &c., Drook House, Rochdale, Feb. 28. J. HOIN ES.

Mr. DARBYSHIRE moved that the services of Miss Bar- low, the assistant seamstress at the Workhouse be discon• I i continued n a week's time. Miss Barlow, he said, was ap- pointed some years ago for a few weeks to help over a tem- porary stress of business, but ha services had been con- tinued up to the present time. Not only that, but he was sorry to say the services of Miss Barlow had been paid for when not rendered. He thought, therefore, that the time had come when her services could be dispensed with.—The CHAIRMAN pointed out that the resolution Mr. Derbyshire bad moved had practically been put in force, as the new matron was to undertake the work of seamstress without 1 paid assistance.—Mr. DARBYSHIRE : Then I am satiafied.- 1 Mrs. MACKEY explained that Miss Barlow bad been there for I some length of time because she (Mrs. Mackey) required [ the services of her or some other seamstress. The House Committee knew of the continuance of her services, as her bills were put forward every month, and she (Mrs. Mackey) presumed the Guardians also knew. It would be a very difficult thing to do without a seamstress at that Workhouse. Referring to the charge that Miss Barlow had been paid for services not rendered, Mrs. Mackey said the money bad been repaid.—This subject then dropped, and the relief cases were proceeded with.

div.head: VOYAGE TO MELBOURNE.
div.p: A VOYAGE TO MELBOURNE.

BY RICHARD RAWCLIFFE. Below is the .conclusion of the Journal kept by ' thg late Mr. Richard Rawcliffe, of Blackburn, during the voyage from London to Melbctime in the Orient Line Royal Mail Steamship Ga ronne. The second portion of the Diary appeared in last Saturday's Examiner. "Wednesday, Sept. 29th.—The weather agahr is very hot, and we are approaching the island of Diego Garcia. Very shortly we anchor close by. It is an interesting place for a European who has never before been outside of Europe, as cocoa nuts and almost all kinds of tropical fruits, spices, &c., grow there. The island is uninhabited, save by men who are employed by the Madagascar Government, and also by the Orient S.S. Company, who have likewise a share or ;interest in the place. We are staying a few hours in order to give out stores to men engaged on the island. I have just seen two large albatrosses, also some devil-fishes, so the sailors called them. Many expressed I a wish to go ashore, but were not allowed, as there was no port, hut or tenement in view. Hundreds of cocoa nuts we saw floating in the water. A few blacks came across in a little steamboat belonging to the Orient Co., and sold coral, shells, &c., to the passengers. The island, which is composed entirely of coral, looked grand in tropical scenery. The sooner we weighed anchor I thought the better, however; for I felt the effects of the intense heat that came from the island. But the blacks were busily engaged trading With the passengers, and very large and ornamental lumps of coral were sold at a shilling each, and half-pint bottles of little thick shells of innumerable shapes and colours, fit for watch appendages; ornaments at a shilling each also. We weighed anchor at 11 a.m. 430 p.m.—A heavy shower of rain, which, being the only one since we left London, is really delightful. After the downfall all is very pleasant, cool, &c., and the passengers generally are in good 'health. lam quite sure I am the most unhappy person or thing abroad, barring a skylark that a man is trying by nursingto keep alive. The weather has been too hot for it, and', as I have just told the owner, I think it will not live until morning. Thursday, Sept. 30th.—The weather is now very squally, and the water is constantly coming on deck. I think we are getting rather easily through the tropic of Capricorn, as the thermometer last night registered only 82 in the shade. As I prognosticaed, the lark died in the night time, and the owner seems to be very sorry about it. He has, however, about a dozen birds left, chiefly canaries, very pretty ones, and a grey linnet —a beauty. The latter is, and always has been since coining aboard, very lively, and, I think, even more likely to get across than myself, as it is in far better health. 530 p.m.—We pass a large sailing vessel far in the distance. Friday, October lst.—Another squally morning with rain, and odd passengers sick. The heat only registered 80 in the shade. I see by a notice posted up on the hospital walls on deck that a club is formed, called the G.G.A.C., or Grand Garonne Athletic Club, by a number of young men. Money has been subscribed, and sports are announced to take place, consisting of hurdle leaping, flat raping, jumping, sack racing, &c., today, to-tnorrow, and Monday, weather permitting. Entrances, prizes, and, in fact, every detail has been gone through in order to make the affair a success. Noen.—Weather windy, ocean rough, the water frequently coming on deck, driving every one out of the forecastle. I foggy, dark, drizzly, wet and dirty afternoon, or, what the Colonists aboard call "proper English weather." Still the sports did take place, and those who could see what was going on seemed to enjoy themselves, judging from 'the loud laughter produced. I was below, out of the I damp, by doctor's orders. "Saturday, Oct. 2nd.—Went on deck as usual to have a wash at 6 N a.m., but had not been long there when the water came right over, and I was wet through, and everyone I think on deck got drenched more or less. I retired to bed, have just got up, and the waters are as rough as ever. The vessel is going slowly, for yester- day she only proceeded 259 miles, her best road record since starting being 304. I told the doctor just now I thought I felt worse, but he did not seem to think se. The eyes look bright,' he always says. Some poet—l forget which just now—says,' The eyes are the windows of the soul,' and it seems the doctor gauges one's health by them. "Sunday, Oct. 3rd.—Yesterday finished as it began— rough sea—so rough indeed that few ventured on deck. This morning is much the same. The chief topic of con- versation just now is about landing. We are expected to arrive at Cape Luin about Thursday next, Adelaide the Thursday after, and Melbourne Saturday night week, so that, if all goes well, we shall leave the vessel on the 16th October. That being so, we shall have been on board 46 days. 1 p.m.—Fresh wind, changed from stern to port side of vesseh Sun come out, and have rather pleasant sailing. We are still only creeping alohg, as yesterday we had proceeded 241 miles, while, to-day only 230 miles. 6 p.m.—The wind is rising, and already the waters are very rough, for the Garonne is rocking as she never rocked before during the voyage. , Everyone moving about deck appears drunk, and cer- tainly everyone is incapable—of walking perpendicu- larly. I have just seen what ought not to be, especially on a Sunday— a fight between an Englishman and an Irishman, but fortunately for both, through the ship heaving so much, neither of the combatants got hurt. They both struck out very hard, but hit nothing, when the boatswain, who seemed to want home rule, put am end to the combat. "Monday, Oct. 4th.—Rough weather all night we have had. I was near being pitched out of the bunk,' and I thought the old ark was going over. What a clatter and jingle of pots, tins, and bottles! A man should be very healthy and fatigued in order to sleep under such conditions. Morning has come without much change. We have had very little sun since before we crossed the line. Two or three deputations of pas- sengers have just been to the captain complaining about the grub,' taking with them specimens of potato hash. The captain observed that he was not aware that such stuff was being served out to them, and promised to see the chief steward, and get it altered. As for myself, I have no appetite for most of the " grub " served out, but now and then I receivd from the steward a "tasty bit." Last night some sort of fish pie was brought to me, which I rather liked after tasting it. I put it aside in my cabin thinking of having a good feed Min it this morning but was vexed beyond measure when I discovered that a thief of a rat had taken away the whole of the inside portion. I threw away, through the port hole, the remainder. Well, we must forgive as we expect forgiveness, so I forgive the rat. 6 p.m.—As the afternoon has been a sunny one and the deck dry, the G.G.A.C. sports (2ad day) have been going on. Climbing the rope occupied a long time; then followed the single stick fencing contest with foils and guards, in which I felt much interested, as a good many of the crew took part in it, and most of them had passed a thorough training. An obstacle nee concluded tke proceedings, and it created loud laughter from the lookers on. "Tuesday, Oct. sth.—Squally and cold, though the sun is visible, which improve; the day somewhat. I have just been to the doctor and told him again about the spitting—that the quantity had at least doubled since coming aboard. He told me I looked none the worse, and that it was better out than in. I told him that the doctors at home had held out no hope of my Tecovery a year ago, and he replied that that was a good reason I should get better, and added jocularly that' doctors are generally wrong.' "Wednesday, Oct. 6th.—Rough, cold weather, above and below. I dare not go on deck through the 'extreme cold, so I am, as it were, compelled to remain, like a prisoner, below. I feel I am growing worse in health every day—in fact, I am literally wearing away, and when I go on the top deck, and I am obliged to go often, I have to hold on the railings to prevent the wind, assis- ted by the oscillation of the ship, carrying me right over into the Indian Ocean. "Thursday, Oct. 7th.—Cold wind on deck, and cold draughts of wind below. No better in healfin • ' "Friday, October Bth.—Suffered in the nighr more than ever. The weather is colder still, and the knowing ones say the temperature will be still lower before we arrive at Melbourne. I have just seep the doctor, Who

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly raeeting of this Board was held at I the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. There were I present the Rev. ti. F. Roberts (chairman), Messrs. Blackhurst, Jolhdy, Voisey, Greening, Harrison, Ish- erwood, Strange, Pennington, Brown. Bonnell, Kit- shall, W. Henghton, Clarke, Ratcliffe, Wright, Darbysbire„ Grange, Eckersley, J C. Sutton (clerk) and S. Sutton, (assi:tant clerk) .

HOUSE COMMITTEE. The House Committee's minutes stated that the flour supplied to the workhouse was not satisfactory.—Mr. Gamenew asked what number of inmates there was at present in the workhouse.—The CLERK replied that there were at that time 397 inmates as compared with 377 in the corresponding week of last year.—Mr. HARRISON: Is the workhouse full? The CHAIRMAN said it was not, there was plenty of room.—Mr. BROWN Moved the confirmation of the minutes and paid with regard to the fl mr that during -aimpst.thewheloof the half year they had been exceeding- lir well serred,bat it Was quite possible that sometimes the miller might sc4 have the flour come from his mill in the condition he would altogether like it.—The minutes were confirmed. INDUSTRIAL SOHOOLS COMMITTEE.
The doctor reorted the gener.l health nf the childrea at Padgite Industrial Schools to be very good. SCHOOL FEES COMMITTEE.

This Committee reported that fees had been allowed in 101 cases, 88 of which were old and 13 new.—Mr. HLACKHURST moved, and Mr. GREENING seconded, the adoption of the minutes. In answer to Mr. Harrison, the CLERK said that the number of fees allowed in the corresponding period of last year was 198.—The CHAIRMAN : It seems better all round —Mr. HARRISON was glad to hear it, yet there was a great deal of distress.—The minutes were confirmed. THE COUNTY RATE. The CLERK mentioned that the demand by the county of Chester for that part of the Union which lay in Che- shire amounted to £6l 13i 41. THE IMPERIAL INSTITUTE. With regard to the above Institution a letter which the Chairman bad received was read inquiring it any steps had been taken in furtherance of the project by forming a com- mittee, &c.—Mr. HARRISON: I hope you will be able to give a good account of yourself, Mr. Chairman. (Laughter.)— The CHAIRMAN :laid the matter had been before them at the previous meeting, and it seemed ta be silently carried that the matter remain in abeyance for an indefirnte time. (Laughter.) But he did not see how they could avoid giv- ing an answer to the present comrannication.—Mr. HAR- RISON did not see that it applied to the other members of the Board, as it was directed to the Chairman entirely. He hoped that the Chairman would be able to successfully vindicate his position. (Latighter.)—The CHAIRMAN was afraid he would have to involve the rest of them in his re- ply. He therefore would like an expression of their feeling in the matter.—Mr. HARRISON: Suppose we should all re- main "mum," what then ?—Mr. BLACKHURST thought they would all have plenty to do in connection with local matters during the 'jubilee year. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. HARBYSHIRE said it seemed to him to be out of the proper order of things for a Board of Guardians to take the matter up at all. Their duties began at destitution, and he thought they they should not ro beyond that. He su4gee.ed that the receipt of the communication should simply be acknow- ledged. The CHAIRMAN thought be had sufficiently gathered the sentiments of the Board, and he could reply to the communication in the sense indicated.—Mr. HAR- RISON remarked that the Imperial institute proposal did not seem to have been a fleeces., awl in some places. he was sorry to see, it had been the means of pr.voking some disloyal expression of opinion.—Mr. PENNiNGTON added that the Church House did not seem to be much of a suc- eess either.—The subject then dropped. THE RESIGNATION OF THE WORKHOUSE MASTER.—THE CASE

div.head: OF MRS. MACKEY.
div.p: OF MRS. MACKEY.

The Clerk read the following letter from Mrs. Mackey, the matron at the workhouse, viz. : Gentaemen,—illow me to express my csmplete astanish- tnent at seeing an advertisement in some of the local papsrs for a matron. Seeing that my appointment was s.parate sad prior to that of the master I desire to remind you that his leaving should not be made 0 affect the offioe I hold under you. Had such a course been taken previous to the appoint- ment of either the present master or his predecessor then I should have understood it. I was then corn•Jaratlvely yawl and untried In the service, but now, after a long. arduous, and faithful performance of my duties, and without any Intl- melon whatever that you should advertise for a succossor— This surely cannot be the course the Guardians intend to pur- sue. If, however, it be your ultimate decision, 1 .hats con- sider it a most extraordinary and unjust method of treating an old and well tried public servant Kindly permit me to draw your attention to the law on the matter. page 163, art. 189 witlere the General Consclidated Order states:—' If any master or matron hereafter appointed be husband and wi'e and or..e of them should be dismissed by order of the Com- missioners, or should otherwise vacate his or her offiee, or should die, the other or survivor shall at the expiration of the then current quarter, cease to hold his or her office of muter et* *Wren as the case may be" This shows that ' whets, it master and illttrol are appointed together" I then If one resigns the other may follow Allow me to say , that this law does not apply to my case I wish also to call your atteralrai to the fact that In the case ~f my predecessor. I who was appointed conjointly with her husband, you retained her after her husband's death, and at a time t .0 when they had held office here only about one year. Again In the case of a maste• who left here and went to the B.h•fileict Union, the Guardians there have retained the mat on's services, although the master was 010 upon to resign after serving them only a few years. What you kindly did then surely you are In a position to do now, especially in the ease of a mu holder ser- vant. But, gentlemen, altogether apart from this surely you cannot be so inconsiderate and ungenerous as ,to attempt to deprive me of the position I have held honourably ard Pail- fully for nearly twenty years to the satisfaction of the Guar- dians, and the Local Government Board Inspectors and I bslieve the ratepayers generally without any cause whatever. '1 cannot sufficiently express my astonishment at the course you have already taken, but it is not too late to reconsider the matter and do me that justice which I think you after con- sideration will admit I deserve. I shall be obliged if y is will kindly grant me an interview at your Board o Wnduesday next, when I will explain the m atter more `sially.—l am, gentlemen, your most faithful servant, th A. MAcggy, Hatton." ant Clerk then read a letter Athtatt'6 116 eardcihu been ther e Cceivheaelrmfatil rom the Local Government Board stating that 15iXt. and Mrs. Mackey should not remain in office longer than the 25th Ifarch.—Mr. EtARRISUE was not sur- prised that Mrs. Mackey should feel aggrieved in the matter, but after that letter from the Local Government Board he did not see what the Board could do.—Mr. VOISEY said that as far as he could learn there was a general feeling, both amongst the Guardians and amongst the public in Warring- ton, in favour of Mrs. Mackey. (Hear, bear.) Geeing epoken in high terms of the manner in which Mrs. Mackey had filled the office of matron, Mr. Voisey suggested that the Guardians should express their opinion strongly In favour of Mrs. Mackey being allowed to retain her post-- The CLERK, in reply to queetions, read the Consolidated Order hearing on the point, which stated in effect that when the master and matron were man and wife,when one was dis- missed or died the other should vacate office at the end of the current quarter. He (the clerk), however, pointed out that in such a case as the present Mrs. Mackey could apply to be re-appointed, and be re-appointed if the Guar- dians thought fit—Mrs. MACKEY asked that the lever of the clerk might be read in reply to whico the communication of the Local Government Board stating that both Mr. and Mrs. Mackey were to leave had been received.— The CLERK then rPad the letter re- ferred to. It stated that he (the clerk) presumed that Mrs. Mackey's appointment would be determined also at the end of the current quitter, and it went on to say that Mr. Mackey seemed to be of opinion that his engagement with the Guardians woeld require a two months' notice—Mr. \TOME thought it was ratner a strong way of putting it to say that he presumed Mrs. Mackey would also have to leave. —The CLERK said presumed that, because he was pre- sumed to know what the law was On the matter.—Mrs. Macxur said she bad read the law on-the matter, and , she Mill said that that law did not apply to her, because she had never been re-ationietert since her first appointment in January, 1868. She was not re-appointed after marrying Mr. Mac- key, but had been appointed separately two years prior to Mr. Mackey.—The CLERK stid in the order he bad read be did not find anything to show that it only applied to the masters and matrons who had been appointed together. —Mrs MACKEY said see thought that after twenty years' service, and eau- finding the workhouse is the condition it was when she'came to it, and leaving it in its present state, it was very hard and amounted to cruelty mate :she should be treated in this way. She felt sure that no guardian on that Board would wish to do an injustice or act cruelly towards her. (Hear, hear.) —The unatnetere said she could see that she had the sym- pathy of every member of the Board, and if they could do her a kindness they would ; but he was afraid that Mrs Mackey's view of the legal aspect of the case was not the correct one. He, however, suggested that a letter should be 'rattail to the'Local Government Board pointing out the excellent way is which Mrs Mackey had done her work, and expressing the regret of the Guardians that the case should- be such a hard one as far as she was concerned.— Mr. Vomit moved that a resolution be passed and sent to the Local Government Board to the effect that the Guar= dians would be glad to find that some coarse could be taken whereby Mrs Mackey might be allowed to retain her posi- tion as matron, If that bad not the desired effect they could do no more.—The CHAIRMAN : I am afraid the Local Government Board would reply that that would be contravening the law.—Mr. HARRISON seconded Mr. Vol- sey's propositiom—Mr. BROWN did not think it would be the right thing to have Mrs Mackey as the matron of that house—a married woman with her husband and children Parted from her, and some other genVernan master of the house.- (Hear, hear.) He stood second to none on that Board is his wish to do anything they could for the benefit of Mrs Mackey, and if they could suggest anything in the shape of an annuity or superannuation to which Mrs Mackey might be entitled, he would les quite agreeable. He was extremely sorry to Part with Mrs. Mackey, but to retain her on audh terms as hail been sug- gested would not, he thought, be wise or advantageous to that workhouse. He was desirous that they should have man and wife as master and matron. He moved an a- mendment to the effect that the Local Government Board , be eked te allow a grant as some recognitiou of MreeMac- I key's services.—Mr. JOLLEY seconded this amendment, and ! said he would-mos heap-arty to separating Mrs. Mackey from her husband and children.—After a little further con - versationilfr. VoudeY withdrew his proposal in favour of that of Mr. Brown.—Mr..DAnEYSIIIRE, however, moved that no letter be Sent from that Board to the Local Govern- ment Board., lie thought such a coarse would bo useless, and besides he would object to superannuation being granted to the matron of that workhouse. Let them continue in the

admits that I am a great deal worse, and has quill' more medicine. "Saturday, October 9th.—The wind has settled down' a little, and the sun has come out. I have managed to crawl on deck with my chair (11 a.m.), but feel to weak as yet to wash. We are expecting to arrive at Cape Luin to-morrow. The old ship has gone ahead at a quicker pace the last 24 hours, she having covered 302 miles of ocean without a stitch of canvass. "Sunday, October 10th—I have not been to bed the last night, having sat up on a chair in my berth, only a wretched way for a sick person to pass the night. Yet, though I was cold, I did manage to snatch about a , couple of hours sleep, which is better than no sleep at all. Getting on deck at 6 a.m. I find we are sailing ' round the Australian coast. The morning is: cold and dull, with some rain and plenty (too much) of wind. 9 a.m.—We have just passed Cape Luin, and are now passing some romantic scenery—an agreeable change. Two rocks alongside each other stand out in bold relief amid the waters on the larboard side of the vessel, .the white-crested waves lapping the very tops throtbe turbulency of the ocean. 4 p.m.—We have been ping most beautifully wild scenery of barren, rocky land the_ whole of the day, and, as night draws nigh, there is no appearance of an end of them in view—hundreds eif miles of coast without the shadow of any living being, save the sea birds which hover around base and brow, where they can rear their broods without any apparent interruption. "Monday, Oct. llth.—The weather is bitterly cold, and I still keep getting worse. "Tuesday, Oct. 12th.—No change in the weather. We are expecting touching Adelaide to-morrow. I have got through another long night in the chair, coughing and shivering with the cold. If I could get a sup of warm tea in the night-time, or a fire that I could draw nearer to, I should feel a benefit from them. Still I must not despair. Hope points to the future and says nothing about the present. A long )vay off even yet, for a day brings more pain now than a week at the be- ginning of the voyage. "Wednesday,' Oct. 13th.—Passed the night in the chair as usual. The weather remains very cold It is too cold to go on deck, and too cold to remain below. Still I feel rather better this morning, as the doctor has got me nourishments, and, indeed, has behaved to melikeatruegentleman from the start. He has drawn me away from the inferior food served to the steerage passengers, and ordered the chief steward to give me special food. In fact lam living like the aristocracy live, so far as food goes now, had I only an appetite to eat what they bring. "Thursday, Oct. 14th, 5 30 am.—We have just dropped anchor at Adelaide, and got notice that anyone wishing to go ashore can do so, as we stay six or seven hours, and soon two boats filled with passengers are seen plying shorewards. Vendors of apples, oranges, &c., were soon aboard doing a brisk trade. 3 p.m.—Off we go again! I feel somewhat little lighter in spirits, know- ing we are a good many days' marches nearer, at least, our new home. This day has been fine so far, but, as the good ship sails away from the port of Adelaide, we are told that a storm is coming on. lam better rather in health than I was a few days ago, for which I feel thankful, and I do hope to do better when I get ashore, not only for my own sake, but for the sake of wife and family I leave so far behind. 5 p.m.—What a change in the weather in two hour's time. It has become so cold one might suppose oneself in Lapland. "Friday. Oct. 15th.—No change in the weather. We are all eager to land. , "Saturday, Oct. 16th.—Hurrah I for the end of the voyage is near, and lam still alive. I - long to be laid down in a proper bed with some friend to nurse ins. At one o'clock, p.m., the vessel arrived at the port of Mel- bourne, and, as the passengers were leaving the vessel and I was looking after my boxes, Mr. Frank Crossley hailed me. He is the son of Mr. James Crossley, portrait and landscape painter, formerly of Branch-road, Black- burn, and a member of the Blackburn Literary Club. Mr. Frank came out during the big strike, and on arrival had nothing to do for some weeks, when a friend learnt him shoemaking, at which trade he is still working and doing well. He conducted me to his house in Mel- bourne, and supplied me with a good tea. Afterwards to the train per tramcar, and I was off at 7 p.m., and arrived at my new home thoroughly exhausted at 12 30, Sanday morning, Oct. 17th, 1886."

OUR LONDON LETTER.
LONDON, THURSDAY.

Ex-minister 4 at the Speaker's dinner last night, and subsequently the larger number of prominent' Liberals who assembled at Mils Peel's levee, were disturbed by an odd apprehension. The Ministry, since the session opened, have been going from bad to worse, and have to-day reached an almost critical situation. What, with one exception, the leaders of the Liberal party most deprecate is-a defeat of the Government in the present session. The ex- sception is Mr. Gladstene who, in his bounding youth and chronic light-heartedness, is ready, iI need be, to face a general election, confident that ' rI the country has already had enough of a Conserva- tive Ministry. But the general desire •is that the present Ministry may at least weather the pre- sent session, and may come up for judgment at the beginning of the next. Three things have happened within the past week which have seriously tended to hasten. the impend- ing fall. One.is the revolt in the Post Office against Mr. Itaikes in consequence of his peculiar form of patronage. This is, of course, not an exceptional episode in the yet brief history of the present Gov- ernment. Lord Cranbrook, it will be remembered, got a ne,ar relative of .his made Clerk of Parliaments in the House of Lords in despite of the well-estab- lished claim of poor Sir Erskine May. That, it is true, wag in a former Government, but it was prac- tically composed of the same men, who now have , in their hands the dispensation of places of profit. Lord Halsbury's career as Lord Chancellor, has been systematic in its promotion of personal connections and political tartisans. • But Mr. R,aikes' conduct affects'the course of the very life blood of one of the most important departments of the State. It has been Continuous and systematic, and draws forth a protest only when marked by a peculiarly flagrant act. Another heavily damaging blow to the Government is the disclosure of the iniquities of the Corporation in which the First Lord of the Admiralty is shown to have had a hand. Lastly there comes the letter from Lord Lymington dis- &sing the little rift within the lute of Dissentient Liberalism which, slowly widening, will make mute the strangely assorted majority that keeps the! Government in power. The Government, discredited by the action of its members, is threatened with desertion by its allies, and, of course, the moment these withdraw their support, the Ministry will fall. But to that end, at least for the present ses- sion, the leaders of the Liberal Party will not wit- tingly assist. Mr. Chamberlain's letter to the "Baptist," like Mr. Bright's vote against the interests of Disestab- lishment in Wales, has completed the measure of angry disgust • with which his co:induct has been viewed. Like Mr. Bright's vote, it would have been so easy not to write the article! But Mr. Chamber- lain is not the man to deny himself the pleasure of hitting out at th-. friends he has dissociated himself from, whenever 'opportunity. arises. I hear from those who frequently come in personal contact with him that there is something actually savage in his temper when he alludes to his former colleagues, or to his present posit/cm relative to the Liberal party. At promiscuonsdinner tab las he holdsfort,h,through all the courses, in bitter denunciation of those he has elected to make his adversaries. On Mr. Labou- chere in particular—and here not without reason— the fullest vials of his wrath are poured fotth. Time was when the ,member for Northampton was one of his choicest companions. But that was the time when Mr. Labouchere used to swear by Mr. Cham- berlain, extolling him in the pages of "Truth,' and hailing him chief' in the House of Commons and other places of public resort. Now Mr. Labouchere, knowing the effect his words, whether written or spoken, have, takes a malicious delight in scarifying Mr. Chamberlain, and Mr. Chamberlain with less itstnteness tfran might have beenex'pected from him writhes under the attack. All this is very sad, and bodes ill for that reunion of the Liberal partrfor which Mr. Chamberlain, not less than others, pro- fesses himself =ions. One thing is evident, and

div.head: 41 11,0 Wila
div.p: 41 11,0 Wila

that is that the reunion, whenever it comes about, ; will not be advanced by the personal action of Mr. 'Chamberlain. He will come round only on one of two. conditions. One is that he !shall get his own way; the other that he finds /himself hopelessly driven to the rear in political influence. He will certainly not get his own way. Even if Mr. Glad- stone were inclined to yield, he could not garry, with him the great bulk of the Liberal party in sub- mission to Mr. Chamberlain's absurd assumption of domination. At present Mr. Chamberlain does not seem inclined to yield. But it has often happened in history that when a man most loudly proclaims he will ne'er consent he is on the point of consent-

ing. The war scare the Continent has distinctly fallen away during the last week, public opinion doubtless being -.influenced by the results of the elections in _Germany. Just itow apprehensive glances are turned in the direction of the east of Europe, rather than the west. Russia is once more . _ .

the Centr6 Of.suspicion, 'and there is talk of active interposition in Bulgaria that may lead to momen- tous events. In the meantime we hear very little of General Boulanger, who seems temporarily to have retired into that seclusion for which he has so little taste. I hear from one intimately acquainted with the course of affairs in Paris that this new

attitude is the result of pressure put upon him by the Ministry. There is a good deal of jealousy in the highest circles of the prominent position as- sumed by the War Minister, and he has found it prudent, for whatever brief period,. to efface him- self. General Boulanger by the way, greatly, affects the company of the correspondents of the London Press in Paris. The great Blowitz has remained implacable; but it (will be observed that the other correspondents of the Lon- don morning papers are almost enthusiastically friendly. Boulanger, unlike most of the French Ministers, speaks English. His mother was an English woman, his father being an advocate who struggled with adverse circumstances at Nantes. There is a story told of Boulanger, illustrative of his vanity, to the effect that when he was a boy he pas- sionately desired the possession of lemon kid 'gloves. There being no funds, forthcoming from the paternal treasury, the boyish-- buck went with- out his luncheon for several consecutive days till he had saved enough money to buy the gloves. Next, per** to the birthday gatherings at the at the Foreign Office, the London season presents no such pretty sight or attractive company as is found at the receptions of the Speaker's wife. From 'a spectacular point of view, ttfe Foreign Office hasthe advantage, inasmuch as diplomatists appear in full uniform, with stars and orders flashing from eltery point of view. There are also among the guests ;military and naval officers in full uniform. At the receptions in the Speaker's court, the only uniforms are the sufficiently handsome ones which Ministers and ex-Ministers wear on special occasions. Last night Mr. Gladstone, looking bright and handsonie' in his ministerial uniform, lingered for some time. Mr. Gladstone always looks well in uniform, best of all in his robes as Chancellor of the Exchequer, which, whatever be the fate of Ministries, he will never more wear. It is only ex-Ministers who have dined with the Speaker who wear their uniform •at the subsequent reception by the Speaker's wife. Thus Lord Herschel, in ordinary evening dress, moved about among the groups of his former colleagues, brave in gold-braided uni- form, with heavy epaulettes and sword—it is to be hoped of better metal than the bayonets served out to the British' soldier., I think the pnncipal tonic of conversation was Lord Lymington's letter on the position of the Dissentient Liberals towards le Government. Its importance was generally O- mitted, for it is presumed Lord Lymington • would not take upon himself to issue such a manifesto except in concert with his pcfttical associates. But the recurrent inquiry was, who wrote the letter P.: The authorship is generally attributed to Lord Lymington's mother, the Countess of Portsmouth, a very able woman. Opinions differ on this point, but there is a conseffsus of belief that Lord Lyming- ton himself was not equal to suoh a literary pro- duction. It is quite true that a kind of pressure is to be put :on the bar to make its members subscribe to the Imperial Institute, and it is quite true that the bar don't at all like it. When I speak of pressure, what I mean is that the Attorney and the Solicitor Generals are to make the appeal. Now, there is a most laudable desire on the part of rising young barristers to stand well with the heads of their pro- fession. This is quite as it should be, and there are many reasons for it. One reason is that`there are so many nice little bits of patronage in the gift of the Attorney General. Happily the present law, officers are not - courtiers. The Attorney General certainly is not. I don't think he cares much about the Imperial Igstitute. Had it been Sir Henry James the bar subscription would have been heavier. _

Such a season as this seems to be for yellow flowers. We have only just got into Spring. The March wilds have not yet begun, but the streets are full of jonquils and daffodils. The trade done is very considerable, and It is quite a new trade. The 4onquils come, some-from France, some from Belgium. The Riviera gives us very little, chiefly those red anemones and the early mignon- ette. The daffodils are English grown. All kinds of country greeneries, too, are sold in the town—twigs and sproutings of shrubs, ivy suckers, yards of trailing creeper, branchy weeds, hitherto protected by their ugliness. The harvest is relent- lessly gathered in, and the.waste and wantonness of destruction is great.

_ The Lord Chancellor took his seat shortly after 40. p.m. THE CHURCH PATRONAGE Bitt.—The Archbishop of Carrel/soar moved the second reading of the Church Patronage Bill. It was based on two principles—Aspely, the declaring of advowsons as a sacred trust, and the giving of the parish power to bring evidence before the bishop as to the fitness of any person who might be nom- inated by any patron. While the bill would not do away with the sale of advowsons altogether, it would provide safeguards which would prevent theirieing used for pur- poses of mere pecuniary profit, and would enable the bishops to refuse the appointment of unfit persons.— Lord GRIMTHORPE moved the rejection of the bill,declar- ing it to he the most revolutionary ecclesiastical measure which had been intrcoluced since the Long Parliament. As a whole private patronage was much better exercised than episcopal patronage. The debato was adjourned until Thursday. RAILWAY AND CANAL TRAFFIC.—Lord STANLEY of Pursrox presented a bill for the regulation of railway and canal traffic, which was read a first time. The noble Lord postponed his explanation of its provisions until the second reading. Their Lordships adjourned at 810 p.m. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MowDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at 4 p.m. The Liverpool, Southport, and Preston Junction Rail- way Bill, the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway Bill, and the West Lancashire Railway Bill were read a second time. ARCHBISHOP CROKE AND TAXPAYING.--Sir M. Him- BFACII said, in answer to Mr. Johnston, that Archbishop Croke's letter from the Palace, Thurles, of date February 17th, countenancing a campaign again against payment of taxes, and setting forth that "our money goes to feed a gang of needy and voracious lawyers, and to purchase bludgeons for policemen," &c., was engaging the atten- tion of the Government. Tun JUBILEE HOLIDAT.—Mr. W. H. SMITH, replying to Mr. Johnston, said her Majesty had promised to attend a jubilee service at Westminster Abbey, on Tuesday, the 21st June, and suitable arrangements would be node for the occasion. It was the intention of the Govern- ment to recommend that the day should be observed as a general holiday. SUPPLY.—THE CIVIL SERVICE ESTIMATES. _ .

—.- The House went into Committee on the Civil Service Supplementary Estimates, Mr. Courtney taking the chair. —On the supplementary vote of ,E 825 for the mainte- nance and repair of Marlborough House, Mr. BRADLARSII said the cost of the Royal Family ought to be included under one head.—Mr. CONYBEARE asked why the. Prince of Wales did not pay for the repair of his own house.—For the vote 209, against 99; majorityfor, 110. On the supplementary vote of £8,200 for the Houses of Parliament, Sir HENRY ROSCOE said they were thoroughly satisfied with the work done, and believed members would not suffer from the smells which afflicted then last year.—Dr. TANNSR called attention to' the frequent "fogginess" of the atmosphere in the House. The air should be filtered through successive lavers of cotton wool. A vote of £9,275 for the maintenance and repair of public buildings was agreed to after discussion by the Irish members; as was the vote of £BOO for the new Admiralty and War Offices. On the supplementary vote of £15,900 for tedipldmatie and Consular buildings, Mr. LAISOIICRARN moved its re- duction by the sum of £14,300, being the cost of the freehold of the site of the Legation House at Brussels.— Mr. Purim= said this transaction would effect a saving instc ad of increasing expenditure.—The amendment was negat ieed.—Mr. LABOGCHERE moved to reduce the vote by L'soo,on account of the purchase money of a house and furniture for the Agent General at Cairo. Considering that we were maintaining the Khedive on the throne, he ought to give us one of his palaces. (Laughter.)—Sir W. atecounv said the late Government had decided against thisproposal, and he objected to it on principle, knowing that the building of a house was not an econo- mical proceeding. (Laughter.)—Mr. JACKSON said Sir R Baring was not in a position to entertain anybody at present without tending out the menibers of his family. —Mr. H. Foserace remarked that although the estimated cost was £27,000, he said that £50,000 would not cover it —Mr. JACKSON stated that by voting the £5OO now asked, the House would be committed to the whole scheme.—Dr. TANNER considered that the voting of this sum would be an indication that the Tory Govern- ment intended to permanently occupy Europe— (laughter)—he meant Egypt.—On a division the amendment was rejected by 153 votes to 22. Several votes were passed, after much discussion hy the Irish members. Mr. Healy and other Irish members were repeatedly called to order for irrelevancy. Colonel NOLAN moved to report progress/—Mr. W. FL Stunt opposed the motion, which was withdrawn, but an attempt to pass further votes was unsuccessful.— Mr. W. H. Spawn said the Government would take a division as a protest against this waste of time.—The committee divided—For reporting progress, 93; against, 212. Mr. DimArrt; moved that the Chairman do leave the chain—Mr. W. H. Stuns contented to report progress. SeveraLltills were forwarded a stage. Mr. Addison brought in a bill to render the owners of dog's liable for injuries done to any person by such dogs, and a, bill to compel a prosecutor to find security for costs in cases arising under section 2 of the 30th and 31st years of Victoria, chapter 35. The House adjourned at 220 a.m. HOUSE, OF LORDS.—TIIRSDAT.
The Lord Chancellor took his seat at 4 15 p.m. ELECTRIC LIGHTING.--TITE MARQUIS OF SALIS- BURY ON PAST LEGISLATION.

Lord TrItIRLOW moved the second reading of the Elec- tric Lighting Act (1882) Amendment Bill, and reminded their lordships of the gambling spirit. which followed the inventions which made lighting by incandescent electric lamps, and of the action of the Government in establishing by the Act of 1882 rules and regulations which had the effect of arresting the floti of capital into all kinds of hasty and ill-considered schemes. The bill for which he now, asked a second reading was founded upon the measure of last year, as it emerged in its amended fOrm from the select committee, and one of its principal objects would be to remove the discouragt went to electric lighting enterprise resulting from the 27th clause of the Act of 1882, under which all the plant and machinery of a company, together with the good- will of its business, were subject to be bought up by the local.Authoritv at the expiration of 21 years. ThA Marquis of Ssusnons had never held a single share in an electric lighting company, and looked at the question solely from the public point of view. The history of the question •was really the history of the emotions of a public department. The Board of Trade was' horrified at the.•posit ion in which Parliament found itself in regard to water companies, and not entirely satisfied with the position in which Parliament found itself in regard to gas companies,and seemed to have resolved that they would not allow Parliament to fall into a similar difficulty again. But their praiseworthy precautions were carried to an excessive point, and the legislation of 1882 had stilled the enterprise of those who , wished to introduce electric lighting into their country: Other countries used it for public purposes, but it could not be used here except by public bodies, and by those individuals who could employ their own machinery for the production of the electric current. Public authorities were not generally inclined to make these enterprises up, and they were put into the position of dogs in the manager, for they would not allow companies to carry out an en- terprise which they would not undertake themselves That was not a position that Parliament ought to sup- port. (Hear, hear.) They ought to allow enterprise to have its full swing, to remove the obistables that had hitherto existed, to offer the terms, not which they thought capitalists ought to accept, but which they found they would accept, and by giving rights; which might be generous and large, to procure for the public the full adVantage of those scientific inven- tions which other nations had, and which now by our restrictive policy. we were preventing the people 'of this country from enjoying, without doing any good to the local authorities, who wtre the subjects of our tender solicitude and care. (Hear, hear.) The bill was then read a second time. _

COPYEIOLD ENFRANCHISEMENT. ' The second reading of the Copyhold Enfranchisement Bill was moved by Lord Hommuss. Lord BRAMWELL did not oppose the second reading, as be understood there was a general desire that it should be referred to a Select Committee, but he objected to its compulsory clauses. He considered it most unreason- able that when neither the landlord nor the tenant desired enfranchiseineht they should be compelled to carry it out. The LORD CHANCELLOR admitted that their bill was an improvement on that of last year, anil as it wah.generally admitted that copyhold tenure was bad, and that in the interest of the public it was important that there should be some alteration in the law on the subject he shoal not oppose the second reading, it being understood that the bill was afterwards to be referred to a Select Com- mittee. The bill NellS read a second _time, and, on the motion of Earl Stanhope, was ordered to be referted to a Select Committee. , THE LUNACY LAws.—The House went into Committee on the Lunacy Laws Amendment Bill, and the LORD CHANCELLOR proposed an amendment requiring that except in cases of raving madness the magistrate should see the patient himself before ordering Ins detention in an asylum—Lord SELTIORNE feared that the machinery provided bv the bill would involve COSis which in some cases might prove embarrassing to the operation of the EIHRSCRELL cancurred in that view.—The amendment was inserted, and the bill passed through Committee. The report of amendments to the Solicitors (frelandV Bill was received, and the House adjourned at 6 55.

div.p: RAINFORD PLOUGHING MATCH.

The annual ploughing match at Rainford, which ' bad been twice postponed, on account of the unsettled character of the weather, took place on Wednesday week on land in the occupation of Mrs. Mary Jack- , son. There was a large number of spectators. The contests excited a great deal of interest, and every- thing paPsed of in a most successful manner. The judges, who were as follows, performed their task most satisfactorily :—Messra John Cropper (Halsall), Joseph Faircluiegh (Wrightington), and Joseph Dean (Upholhend)., After the match a suostantial dinner was served at the Eagle and Child, an 4 the chair at the subsequent proceed- , lags was occupied by Mr P Middliehurst, and the vice-chair . by Mr Thurston Fairhurst. The proceedings were of a very pleasant character. The contests aod the lists of winners were as follows :—For first-014,es ploughmen (open to all England)—First prize £5, second prize £3 10e, third prize £2, fourth prize £l, &di, prize 103. For second-class ploughmen (for men who have not won a prize of the value of £4 since January' 1884)—First prize £4, second psize £3, third prize £2, fourth prize £l, tifth prize Iss, sixth prize 10e. For third-class ploughmen (for men who reside in It ainford or Bickerstaffe, who have never got a pr:ze value £2)—First prize XI, and a horse cloth, value £1 2t, presen- ted by Mr Peck, Wigan; second prize, a horse cloth, value Li 25., presented by Mr Baldwin, Wigan; third prize 10s. The executors of Mr II Ball, Itainford, presented a halter, value £1 2s, to the ploughman who had the neatest and cleanest turnout as regarded person, horse, and harness, the harness not to be new, and else a second prize of Ioe. This claws was confined to tenant farmers. Mr Rogerson gave a macintosh value £1 lOs for the most valuable pair of horses . engaged in the ploughing match, being the property Cf one person, and also a second prize of 103. div.head: ,HOUSE OF COMMONS.-TIIEBDAT.
div.p: ,HOUSE OF COMMONS.-TIIEBDAT.

The SPeakerstook the chair at 4 p.m. Inxsu MeansruArns AND THE SUPPRESSION OF MEET. nrGs.—ln reply to Sir T. Femonde, who on rising to put his question was greeted with loud Home Rule cheers, Sir M. HICKSLBEACH said local justices of the peace Ireland were not the sole judges as to the legality-of meetings, nor had they, the right to suppress public meetings indiscriminately.—ln answer to a further

Lord Ck. HAMILTON said Sir R. Fowler had denied the allecations made ngainst him—(cries of "no "I —at any rate he had authorised him (Lord G. Hamilton) to deny them for him. As to the course the Government were prepared to take they were ready to grant an inquiry, but would not confine it to the acts of any one .body or association.

Mr. GLAnstromt, who rose amid loud Opposition cheers, said whatever inquiry was granted must be one into the proceedings of both sides, but it must alsD be an inquiry into specific charges. (Hear, hear.) It was alleged that public funds had been used by a public body for a corrupt purpose. It was a charge of a misuse of nubile trust against the greatest Corporation in the kingdom—that was the matter at issue, and it was that into which the House expected the inquiry to be made. If any such charges were made against the Municipal Reform League by all means let them be gme into, but the question now before the House was the.misapplica- tion of public funds by the Corporation of London. He would advise his hon. friend (Mr. Howell), to state his charge in a definite form in writing, so that the Govern- ment might be able to make a definite answer as to the inquiry they would institute. Mr. W. 11. Swim, 'replying to the right hon. gentle- man, said that if Mr. Howell would take the course just suggested the Government would consider the matter, and would indicate the course they would be prepared to take. As to the constitution of the proposed com- mittee it appeared to him that in a matter of this kind the committee .should be nominated by the Committee of Selection, and that no party elementshould be allowed to appear in tlae constitution of that body. , .Mr. Hownt here asked whether the Government were prepared to agree to the following motion, of which he would give notice:—" That a select committee be appointed to inquire into and report on certain charges brought to the notice of this House by Mr. Howell and Mr. Bradlaugh, alleging the improper use of and malversation of public funds by the Corporation of London, by and with the consent of members and officials of the said Corporation, with power to administer paths, and compel the attendance of persons and the pro- duction of books and papers." (Cheers.) Mr. W. H. SMITE' suggested that the motion should , appear in print on the paper on the following day, and ! stated that on Thursday 116 should be prepared to state what course the Government would take upon it. Mr. GLADSTONE thought the demand made by the Go- vernment in regard to the serious charges that had been I made a fair one, and advised its acceptance. Mr. How= concurring, the motion for adjoutnment was withdrawn, and the orders of the day proceeded with.

Mr. Leake pro- posed to amend this proposal by declaring that the person putting the closure in motion should be a member of the Government, the mover or seconder of the motion then in debate, or the mover or seconder of an amendment thereto. On a division Mr. Leake's amendment was defeated by 291 to 119.—Mr. Wwirnnatin then moved to omit the words "unless it shall appear to the chair," and contended that if they were to adopt the closure it ought to be in as simple a form as possible.—The debate was adjourned on itiie motion of Mr. Slum. The Battersea meeting cost upwards of £6O, there being no item for advertisements or posters, which were not needed as the audience was hired. div.head: GENERAL NEWS.
div.p: GENERAL NEWS.

An explosion occurred at. the Thurso Gasworks on Monday, by which the manager, Mr. Young, lost his life. It was caused by the bursting of a bode; which blew the house to pieces. Mr. 'Young wad found among . the ruins, and died in half an hour.

A Birroama SENT TO Prusox.—A Birkenhead butcher, named John Taylor, who had deposited in the Corpora- tion slaughter-houses the carcases of two calves, which, if used as food, mfght have produced serious results, has been sent by Mr, Preston to gaol for a month's hard labour. A panic occurred at the Gospel Institute, Ilutherglen, during service on Sunday night. A woman raised the cry of" Piro" on observing some smoke. There was an immediate rush to the doors, many being severly crushed in escaping. The smoke came from an adjoining chimney. JEALOUSY AND ATTEMPTED MIIRDER.—LatO On Satur- day night Richard Goodlaw stabbed in the temple a woman named Berry, an assistant at the lodging-house where he resided, at Chatham, with a butcher's knife, through jealousy. The woman is in the hospital in a dying condition. HORBE9 Non Tun AEMY.—Orders have been given at the War Office for a committee of officers to assemble there shortly under the presidency of General Sir Arthur Herbert, K.C.B. Quartermaster-general, to consider the number of horses required by staff and regimental officers for service in the field.

THE BRITISH ASSOCIATION AND MANCHESTER:A local guarantee fund of £9,000 has been raised for the next meeting of the British Association to be held in Manches- ter in August. The new Owens College Museum and reception-room, and many great factory works will be thrown open for the inspection of the visitors.

Applications from many volunteer corps have already been received by the military authorities for permission to attend the Easter manoeuvres, in association with the regular troops at Portsmouth, Dover, and Aldershot, and there is good reason to believe that the total number of men under arms on Easter Monday will reach 50,000.

THE SISTERS OF TH7I POOR CASE.—Miss AllcarcPs solici- tors have served notice of appeal on Miss Skinner, the Mother superior of the Sisters of the Poor, from the decision of Mr. Justice Kekevrich refusing to direct the return of several thousand pounds given by Miss•Alleard to the convent during her residence there as a sister. Bunts nst DISTRESS.—At a meeting on Saturday of the : local committee appointed to. make arrangements for the expected visit of the Royal Agricultural Society to Not- tingham next year, several large landowners excused themselves on account of the bad times from subscribing to the guarantee fund. Amongst these were the Duke of Portland and the Purse of Rutland. THE MANCHESTER MURDF.ROI:IS GANG—Owen Callaghan was on Saturday remanded at Manchester for being con- cerned in thatuurder of Joseph Brady, in that city, on the sth instant. Four persons have already been com- mitted in connection with the murder of Brady, who was stabbed while defending himself in the street from an unprovoked attack. At Manchester, on Monday, Chas. Burton. a well-dressed young man, was charged with throwing vitriol at Harriet Riley. The prisoner had been engaged to the prosecu- trix, but when he fell out of work she broke off, the engagement. He begged her to resume the engagement, but she refused. He then took a bottle containing vitro' from his pocket, and during a struggle sorne of it went on her face, producing indelible scars. - -

, On Monday, a deputation from a body described as the Lord's Day Observance Society waited upon Mr. Plunket, Chief Commissioner of Works, to protest against boat- ing being permitted on Sundays in London parks. Mr. Plunket, after listening to several members of the depu- tation, said he should not think of rescinding the order permitting Sunday boating, for. as far as he had seen, no harm had arisen. The deputation retired much dissatis- fied. and threatening that the matter would be brought before Parliament.

DEFECTIVE BAYONETS.— The committee on defective sword bayonets met at the War Office on Saturday; Sir llussey Vivian, M.P., presiding. Captain H. H. Rawson, of the Indus, guardship of the Reserve at Devonport wbere the bay3nets were first tested and found to be defective; Captain Cleveland, of the gunnery ship Cam- bridge, at Devonport; and Captain Percy Luxmore, of the Dev.astation, were examined. Captain Luxmore produced twenty bayonets which were bent on board his ship, and Captain Rawson produced others from the Indus.

GERMAN IRONCLADS IN Barrisn IVArEns.—Three large German ironclads—Prinz Albert, Steir, and Groth— arrived in Bantry Bay on Friday afternoon, from Ber- muda, and anchored in the position usuaM taken by British war vessels. Early on Saturday rnorrung another German man-of-war arrived in Bantry Bay, and took up her moorings in line with the others. Commodore KaII received orders from Berlin to return to Germany after calling at Queenstown for provisions; but the squadron Was unable to leave through a strong gale raging.

TRU OLDHAM MURDERESS : DATE OF EXECUTION.—The High Sheriff of Lancashire has notified to the governor of Walton Prison that the execution of Elizabeth Berry, sentenced to death for poisoning her child at Oldham, will take place on Monday, March 14th. Formerly all executions in Liverpool were carried out at Kirkdale Prison. The practice in the case of female prisoners will now cease, by order of the Home Secretary, and in future ferrates sentenced to death will be executed at Walton. : :rry will he the executioner.

SIMMS COLLISION IN TIM MERSBY.—VESSSL Si7NIC.— On;Sunday morning, a serious collision occurred in the Mersey, near the Landing Stage, The Locksley Hall, a tine vessel, inward bound from San Francisco, with a cargo of grain and tinned meats, was coming up the river, in tow, and, asshe was rounding in order to enter the Waterloo_ Dock, she collided with the steamer Regulus, and shortiT'afterWards went down. Before she sank, however, PDPkthree passengers, and the crew were rescued. .1.%:L.,„,•-T „ijijk.„,„
