Oxford-street, Manchester.—. Advt. A young lady named Cockayne, of Clarkson-street, Sher- field, was killed on Wednesday afternoon by being thrown from a dogcart in which she and another lady, Miss Witty., were driving at Hollow Meadows, near Sheffield. Miss Witty escaped without serious irjury FATAL FIRE IN RIIIMINGHANLNOt ITHICiI under .£lO,OOO damage was done by a fire which broke out on Wednesday night at the large factory of Mr. Wild, builders' woodwork manufacturer, Charles Henry-street, Birmingham. During the fire a high wall fell upon a row of cottages, and the fall of the debris so is jured several persons who were removirg furniture for friends that five of them had to be taken to the Queen's Hospital, including two young women named Baker, one of whom died fremthe injuries on Thurs- day. RIOTING IN Lunnaw.—Details of serious rioting at Lur- gan have reached Dublin. The police tried to disperse some bands, and a collision occurred with a mob. A crowd of buys pelted the police, and someone fired a pistol at them. The police instantly ran to the barracks for their guns, and the order was given to fire. Four shots were fired, and two persons were very seriously wounded, a Mrs Mulli- ghan-wak shot in the neck, and a girl named Mary M•Veigh was also shot in the wrist by a pellet. Twelve police formed a cordon across Edward-street to prevent Catholic bands porn invading the Protestant quarter. During the affray six persons were arrested and brought before the magistrates. Much damage was done to property, many windows being smashed. Some houses bore traces of bulletl marks. THE RAILWAY FATALITY AT ROBY. An inquest was held at the Seel Arms, Huyton Quarry, by Mr. S Brighouse. county coroner, on Monday afternoon, on the body of John Berns, platelayer, who was killed on Friday last by the Liverpool and Manchester express. After evidence of iden- tification by John Bellis (father of the deceased), William Atherton (platelayer), and Alfred Grayson (engine-driver), deposed to the facts, from which it appeared that the de- ceased and Atherton were trimming the ballast to the out- side of the south up line when the express came upon them, their attention being distracted by the noise of two other trains which were passing at the same time. Grayson said that he noticed the two men whilst passing through Itobv Station. They appeared to him to be clear of the line and watching for the express. He Whistled, but the wind might have carried the sound away. A verdict of "Accidental ‘death " was returned.

Tait KumstnA Site*Mona—The men rescued from the emigrant ship Kapunda, and some of the crew of the Belfast barque Ada Me'more, arrived at Plymouth on Monday night. Their narratives do not materially differ from the accounts already telegraphed of the col- lision and the appalling loss of life which resulted. PUBIFTIEG THE ARMY.--It is stated that 89 8 result-of the most successful recruiting during the past quarter, and with a view to encourage a better class of young men to join the army, the commanders of infantry , battalions at Aldershot have received orders to eliminate 1 from the ranks all bad characters, and unpromising re- crnits.

- FEARFUL ACCIDENT IN SOUTH WALES.—A fearful acci- dent occurred on Monday at the Dowlais Steel Works, South Wales. The men were at work in the pit of the Bessemer department, and a molten mass was being emptied from a ladle into the mould when an explosion took place, the cause of which is not ascertained defi- nitely, but is thought to have arisen from the presence in the mould of water, and four men were seriously burnt.

DEATH-RATE OF TAY 13R/Doss.—ln connection with the placing of the last girder on the new Tay Bridge, it is stated that the loss of life in the building operations is eleven, and that through no fault of the contractors, but solely owing to the men's own carlessness, or from sheer accident. In the building of the old bridge upwards of forty men lost their lives, six of these i being caused by the explosion of the cylinder of an air bell n exca- vating operations. A Sheriff's Court was held at Leicester Castle on Mon- day to assess damages in a breach of promise brought by Miss Lizzie Smith, a dressmaker, against Arthur Tunbridge, corporation clerk. The parties became acquainted in 1883, and the defendant quickly declared undying affection. He was accepted, and arrangements were made for the wedding by special licence at Notting7 ham. Defendant, however, failed to attend. The plaintiff subsequently had a child. A verdict for -£lOO was returned. THE BURY Wraz MURDER.—WaIter Wood, an engine fitter, was charged at Bury Police Court, on Monday, with the wilful murder of his wife, Emily Ann Wood, at Bury, on the afternoon of the 17th February. They had been living apart for some time, and on the 17th ult. prisoner sent her a letter asking her to meet him. She did so, and they walked together to Huntley Brook Farm, where, it is alleged. he deliberately cut her throat from ear to ear. Prisoner was committed to take his trial at the next Manchester assizes. EXCIT/NG SCENE AT A FiRE.—An exciting scene was witnessed at a fire which broke out at the Golden Ball public-house, Nottingham, on Satur- day. The proprietor and family were awakened to a sense of danger by the barking of a dog, and found escape by the stairease completely cut off by flames. An alarm was raised, and the publican, his wife, mother, and children were rescued through the bedroom window by a policeman standing upon the shoulders of two men. The publican was slightly burned, but otherwise escaped uninjured. ANOTHER SHOCKING TRAGEDY IN LONDON:A shocking case of attempted murder and suicide is reported from London. Shortly before six p.m. on Sunday, Rebecca Woodcock, eget:l.l9, of 19, Clayton-street, Islington, was taken to the .University College HospitalThavi ng been shot by her sweetheart, to whom she was to have been married next Sunday. Mr. Heath, the senior surgeon, performed an operation, and succeeded in extracting the bullet from the left temple. At 830 last night the young woman was reported to be recovering consciousness. The man shot himself, fatally. SIR HENRY JAMES ON LIBERAL TJN/TY.--Sir Henry James, acknowledging a letter informing him that he and Lord Herschell had been unanimously elected hon. members of the Manchester Reform Club, says that at any time he should regard the election as a great com- pliment, but under present circumstances the compli- mentary aspect gives way to considerations of a more substantial character. Such combined action by a large number of Liberal politicians seems to make clearer the desirability of doing much to maintain the unity of the party. In this sense he holds the election in the highest 'value. SCENE AT A VOLUNTEER'S FUNERAL.—An extraordi- nary scene occurred on Sunday at a Volunteer's funeral near Newcastle. Some 20,000 to 30.000 people assembled outside Elswick Cemetery gates to witness the funeral. After the gun-carriage had passed inside, the gates were 'shut to keep out the crowd, but the pressure was so great that they were burst open. The people in thousands swarmed over the graves and tombstones, trampling down shrubs and trees, awl doing ,great damage. A number of women and children narrowly escaped being trampled upon, and the clothes of many persons were much torn. Fortunately no one was seriously injured. A PARLIAMENTARY CANDIDATE COMMITTED TO PRISON. —At the Court of Record, Manchester, on Monday, W. Mc.Cruffin Greaves, who unsuccessfully contested one of the divisions of Glasgow at the last general election, was sued by a tradesman named Carey for the instalment of an account for work done.—Plaintiff's solicitor stated that Greaves was one of the citizens' auditors of Man- chester, and a candithte for Parliament at the last elec- tion. He had a restaurant in Manchester, on which he paid £lOO per year in rates; but as the restaurant was in his wife's name, they could not get at him. In a second case, in which Greaves was the defendant, it was stated that Greaves had said fie could pay, but would not until compelled. He did not appear, and in each case the court made an order committing him to prison for seven days, but suspended the operation of the order for 14 days. • VERDICT OF MURDER AGAINST A CONDEMNED WOMAN. —The inquest touching the death of Mrs. Mary Ann Finley, at Castleton, Rochdale, on Fob. 13, last year, Was resumed on alonday, before Mr. Molesworth, coroner. It will be remembered that the body of Mrs. Finley was recently exhumed, owing to suspicions having arisen as to the cause of her death. Evidence was given showing that although the corpse had been twelve months buried it contains a substanl.e believed to be ntropia. a poison extracted from the deadly nightshade. The symptoms prior to death were said tube consistent with poisoning by atropia. A verdict was returned of wilful murder against Elizabeth Berry, Mrs. Finley's daughter. Berry is now. lying under sentence of death at Liverpool, for the Poisoning of her own daughter at Oldham Work- house, and her execution has been fixed for Monday, March 14th. MYSTERIOUS DEATHS us LIVERPOOL.—An inquest was held at Liverpool on Saturday on the body of Michael Murphy. A policeman while passing Murphy's house saw smoke issuing from it. He tried to enter, but was prevented by a man named Doyle, who stood in the door- way. The policeman, however, forced his way into the hoe :e and found Murphy in flames. The stairs and the partitions adjoining were also on fire. Murphy said , Doyle had thrown a lamp at him. He was taken to the infirmary, where he died from his burns. Doyle said he was moving the lamp When it fell and set Murphy on fire. He also made other statemettts of a contradictory character. :Neighbours deposed to hearing men quar- relling end a crash of gI4S. They heard a cry of "Murder," and saw the deceased in flames. The inquiry, was adjourned.—The inquest on the body of the secre- tary of the Garrick Club, Liverpool, Who was found in the Mersey, has been adjourned in consequence of the mysterious circumstances surrounding the case. A COLONEL CONVICTED OF FRAUD—At the Old Bailey, on Monday, Colonel Browning,, late .Pay- master of the Forces, at Chatham, was charged with making false entries in the accounts of his office with intent to defraud. The Attorney-General appeared for the prosecution, and Mr. Lockwood for the defence. The forneet stated that the fraud had been carried on for years, and the prisoner had, by undercasting figures on one side and overcasting them on the other, shown an apparently correct balance. The total deficiency was 1.£3,000. 'One of the principlal clerks at the War Office was examined at considerable length to bear out counsel's opening statement. Yesterday Mr. Lockwood addressed the jury for the defended. He said he should not contend that the mistakes in casting up accounts were the result of accident, but he asked the jury to say that there was no proof of the intention of the defendant to defraud, or that any of the money had ever come into his possession. A number of prominent officers were examined, and gave Cclone/ Browning a high character. Justice qtawkins then summed up to the jery. , He said it was admitted that the defendant had-by means of false figures shown wrong balances, and the only question for the was whether such a state of things would ,have occurred except from a wilful intrition to deceive. The jury immediately- re- turned a vertie, guilty. Mr. Lockwood t'len reminded the court that the defendant would forfeit his pen- sion of £250 per annum, and sentence was postponed WHIT IS KOMPO ? A substitute for intoxicating drinks and a valuable remedy for coda. &c. Directions given with each bottle how to make a Temperance Cordial. No house should be without' it.—Adet. SUSPECTED MURDER OF AN OrvicEß.--The body of a well-dressed, military man, who died in the General Hos- pital, Birmingham, on Sunday, from injuries inflicted under very suspicious circumstances, was on Monchv identified as that of Lieutenant-Colollel George Newton Fendall, com- manding the regimental district of Shrewsbury. The de- ceased officer left Shrewebury on Saturday to attend one of the Birmingham theatres, and upon leaving was seen in company with a woman named Rooney, whom he accom- panied to her home, which is situated in a low court in Baeot-street. Later on he was carrisd from the house in an insensible condition by the woman and a young man named Lester, to a cab, and conveyed to the hospital, where it was found that he had sustained a fracture of the shnll The woman; who gave a false name and address, ascribed his in- juries to a fall. She and Lester were arrested, and have been remanded en a,cbarge of causing the colonel's death. An inquest was opened at Birmingham on Monday afternoon, and adjourned. The body and clothes show evidences of a struggle, and although only a few shillings were found in the pockets, it is known that he had over ZIS when be left Shrewsbury on Satueay. Hie jewellery and an overcoat are also missing. On Wednesday, at the Pollee rourt. the man ' and woman accused of c teeing the death of Colonel Fendal, were brought before the magistrates and again remanded for a week. It appears beyond doubt (says a correspondent) : that the deceaeed was robbed, and the police are convinced • that other persons were concerned in the affair. I THE HIGHEST PRAISE.
A FEW SINCERE AND EARNEST WORDS FROM THE CLERGY.

The fact that a man occupies the responsible position of a religious teacher entitles him to unquestioned respect, and gives his words and endorsements a special power. The statements which follow are voluntary in their nature, and are given because the facts they contain are believed to be of great benefit to the human race. SATIMDAY.—Before Aldermen Burgess and Chand-1;y- DESERTION. —John Eyres, who admitted being a deserter from the Ist Battalion Liverpool Regiment, stationed in Ireland, was remanded to await a military escort. MONDAY. —Before the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere), Ald- erman Liar rison, and Councillors Greening and Francomb. MiscELLesnors:—Thomas Riley, John Joyce, and John Yates were each sent to prison for'seven days for begging. —John Moran was sent to prison for a month for drunk- enness and disorderly conduct, and John McCone was fined 5s and costs for a similar offence. Jane Runcorn, who was also charged with drunkenness, was let off with a caution. —Edward Conner was summoned for allowing an omnibus to stand in King-street, a longer time than was necessary for the loading and unloading of passengers. Mr. A Browne defended. A fine of 5s and costs was imposed.—William and Job Brierley n ere summoned for cruelty te a mare, but as the animal had been destroyed, the case was dismissed.— Ambrose Foden, John Bibby, and Richard Weaver, were each fined for disorderly conduct.—Sidney Cooper. War- burst, butcher, Market-place, was summoned for causing an obstruction by allowing several nieces of meat to hang over the footpath, on the 19th ult. A fine of 20s and costs was im- posed.—James Backhouse, James Shaw, and Tom Lane, were summoned for committing a breach of the peace in the Market-place, on the 19th ult. Defendants offended by standing outside the shop known as the Yorkshire ,Free Trade Butcher's, shouting and ringing a bell in order to at- tract custoni. They were ordered to be bound over in their own sureties of £5 each, and to pay costs...
TUESDAY.—Before Mr. F. Moi2ll-a and Alderman Sutton.

r RUNKENNESS. —Henry Bushell, for having been drunk and disorderly in HOrtireMilltkOt•Street, NYRS fined 5s and costs. —Mark O'Brien, charged with being drunk and disorderly in Arpleproad, and with haying assaulted P.C. Bell, was also fined 5s and costs.
WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. John Fakelough, Alderman Chandley, and Mr. Garnett.

ASSAULT ON i Moran—Daniel O'Loughlin (20), deserib,d as a cornerman, was brcught up in custody on a charge of having assaulted his mother, Mary O'Loughlin, OD the 28th ult.—Mrs. O'Loughlin, an elderly woman, de- posed that when in the house her son commenced being abusive, and knocked her down with a blow on the face. Her face was severely cat, and she had it dressed at the Infirmary. Evidence to a similar effect was given by the prisoner's father, and Inspector Spinks deposed that when he arrested the prisoner the same morning, be (prisoner) used very abusive language. It was his ninth appearance, three of which had been on charges of assault.—The magis• trates sent him to prison for four months, with bard labour. TIIIIRSDAY—Before Major Littou and Alderman Webster.
DRUNKENNESS —Mary Riciardson, charged with being drunk and disorderly ip Scotland-road, was dismissed on promising not to offend again.

DESERTION.—Tbomas Newton admitted being a deserter from Her MajeVy's East Kent Regimen; stationed at Dover. was remanded to await a military escort. FRAUDULENT EALISTMENT.—Johrt Green was charged with making a false answer on being attested as a recruit at Orford_ Barracks. He was remanded.

Two Ronal( CrsromEns.—Bodelia Knockton, a young woman, was chyged with being drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-street on the previous night, and with assault- ing P.C. alernock. Evidence was given to the effect that prisoner was very violent, and had to bo taken into custody; on the way she kicked the constable. There was a black list of previous convictions against her, and the magistrates now seat her to prison for a month for drunkenness, and for three months for the assault.—Paniel Hennessey, a young man, also a well-known character, was brought up in custody on a charge of having been drunk and disorderly on Croppet's brow the same morning, and also with having as- saulted Constables Robinson and Monoghan. The former officer heard a disturbance in the neighbourhood of Crop- per's brow and found prisoner there drunk. Prisoner was also disorderly,, and the officer took him into custody. Prisoner struck him, and the two then had an up and down struggle. Robingon blew his whistle, and Monoghan, who came to his assistance, was also assaulted. Prisoner was committed for a month for drunkenness, and for Biz months for the aes.auit.
FRlDAY—Before the Mayor (Alderman Pieltmere), Dr. Hornell, Captain Reynold, Mr. John White, and Alder- man Harrison.

BEGGING.—Mary Holden, charged with begging in King. street, on the evening pievious, was dismissed with a re- primand. DRUNKENNESS.—Margaret Kißala was charged with being drunk and dismderly in Buttermarket-street on the previous night. bin was fined 5s and costs. FRAUDULIENT ENLISTRIENT.—John Green was brought up on remand on a charge of making a false attestation On enlisting at Orford Barracks. He represented that he bad not been in the service before, which was found to be un- true. Ile was sent to prison for fourteen days.

D/SORDBRLY Womiriv.—Winlfred Conway and Annie Daley were summoned for committing a breach of the peace by fighting in a nnblic•houss in Horsernarket-street on tba 26th ult. Daley and another girl named Margaret O'Brien were also summoned for haying been drunk and disorderly. in Arpley-street on the 23th tilt. O'Brien was fined 5s and costs, Daley was fined Ss and costs and ordered to find a surety to keep the peace for six months, and Conway was fined 5s and costs.—Mary McCoan, charged with being drunk and disorderly in Bridge-street, on the 27th ult., was sent to prison for fourteen days.

THROWING ORANGE PEEL, ON THE FOOTPATH.—Peter Phillips was summoned for throwing orange peel on the footpath in Market-street, to the danger of passengers, en the 26 hof February. When cautioned by P.C. Johnston, defindant became very abusive.; be also gave a false name and address. The Bench imposed a fine of lOs and costs.

PISTOL FIRING.—John Kennon, a young man, was sum- moned for firing off a pistol within fifty feet of the high- way. Sergeant Cheeny said that on the 27th ult., he was on Bank Quay Bridge when he heard the report of a firearm, and easy that defendant, who was on the private ground of the London and North-Western Railway, bad fired a pistol. On bring spoken to by the sergeant, defendant said he was very sorry. The case was dismissed on payment of Costs. A SUNDAY AKIISEMENT. Margaret Grounds, Ellen Adams. and aiaty Moran, young women, were summoned for obstructing the footpath in Gee-street, by playing skip- ping rope, on Sunday. They were each ordered to pay 3s 6d COetfl.

'summoned for being disorderly on the highway at Great Sankey on the 2od ult. Mr. P. Davies defended. The caSte was disinies,d.—Seth Woodl a lad, summoned for being asleep while in charge of a horse and cart, And was fined 2s 81 and costa.

' DRIINEENNESS.—Subn Clayton. for bong drunk and dis- orderly at Poulto' n and Richard Clewer, for being drunk and disorderly at Rix:on, were each fined 5s and costa. Henry Creakie arid Joseph Walmsler were each fined 5s and costa fora similar ( ffence.

ALLEGED ASsA1:11:1'-.--Liii—ree. boys namvd Thomas Ince, Henry Merrick, and Williain Webster, were charged with criminally assaulting Ann Davies, at daydock, on the 27th ultimo, and were remanded on bail until the following day.

.UNMUZZLED DOGS.—A number of persons were summoned for allowing rbob d gs to be at large unmuzaled, and not under proper control. Wjllj4m Grimsbaw and J.imes Ditch. field were each fined is and costs, and charges against Na- polean Bailey and John Rigby were dismissed.

ANTI-VACCINATION PROSECUTIONS. At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday. be- fore Messrs. R. Houghton, C. Pil*agton, and W. P. Gooch, George Owen, Earlestowe, was summoned for neglecting to hive his child Vaccinated. Mr. John Clarke, president of the garlestown branch of the Anti-compulsory Vaccination Society, appeared on behalf of the defendant, and said he was in- structed to say thAt the child . ha 4 not been vac- cinated. Mr. Alfred Cooper, vaccination pincer, was then sworn, and proved having served the usual notice requiring the child to be vaccinate 4. He spoke to defendant about the matter, and defendant said he would not have his child vaccinated.—Mr. Clarke said the defendant had a reasonable excuse for not having it done.—The Clerk: What is the reasonable excuse, Mr. Clarke ?—Mr. Clarke: This man knowing that vaccination does not prevent small-pox, and seeing the serious results which have followed vaccination, dare not risk his child to such results. He therefore has a reasonable excuse, and I would ask your worships to dismiss the case. If your worships cannot see your way to do this, I would ask you to inflict a mere nominal penalty.— The Chairman: The law says children must be vac- cinated, you know.--Mr. Clarke: Yes, but it says also, unless they have a reasonable excuse.—The Magistrates' Clerk (Mr. Nicholson): Your "reason- able excuse" is not a reasonable excuse in the law. It is merely an objection to the Act.—Mr. Clarke: At Leicester it has been admitted. I can produce evidence of that if desired.—The Chairman said the defendant must produce a medical certificate of unfitness—which would be a reasonable excuse.— Mr. Clarke: It has been done in other towns, and - there are a great many towns where they are not enforcing vaccination.—The Chairman said that was very likely.—Mr. Clarke added that there were over 16,000 children unvaccinated in Dewsbury, and over 20,000 at • Leicester. It seemed a very arbitrary thing to enforce it when it did not answer the end expected.—The Bench imposed a fine of 5s and costs. _ _ _

Thomas Gilman, of Earlestown, was summoned for a similar offence, and Mr. Clarke appeared on his behalf.—Mr. Cooper proved the case, and said the defendant when asked if he would have the child vaccinated, said he would please himself.—ln reply to Mr, Clarke, vlritli6s said he took out the summons on the day following that upon which he saw the defendant. —Mr. Clarke; tnd do you con- sider that a reasonable time provided he had repen- ted, and concluded to have his child . vaccinated?— Mr. Cooper:, I did not consider any time necessary after the answer he gave me, and knowing what the man is.—The Chairman: He had plenty of time to have the child Vaccinated. Is it vaccinated now? —Mr. Clarke: No, it is not.—Mr. Cooper: I have reason to believe that he does not intend to have it vaccinated.—Mr. Clarke: I will ask you to deal as leniently with the defendant as you possibly can. No doubt he has a reasonable excuse like the other defendant, and, he cannot submit. —The defendant was fined 5s and costs.—Mr. Clarke: Will your worships allow a little time to pay the money—say a month ?—The Chairman: No.

Replying to Mr. Barran, in the House of Commons on: Monday, Mr. Ritchie gave the Regis- trar-General's statistics showing the death-rate from smallpox in, the districts in which Keighley, Bing- ley, and Leicester are situated, and where the Vac- cination Acts are not' generally complied with. Though the mortality from the disease had been low, it was slightly in excess of other towns he mentioned. But during the last ten years, the Registrar-General reported, there had been no smallpox epidemic in these towns.

div.head: CURRENT POLITICS.
div.p: CURRENT POLITICS.

Lord Hartington has consented to attend the banquet to be given to Mr. Goschen, in Edinburgh, on April 16th. The leaders of the Unionist party in Liverpool have' presented Mr. Goscherrwith a cheque for his election ex- penses in that city. A Cabinet Council was held on Saturday,' in Lord' Salisbury's private room at the Foreign Office. All the Ministers were present, including Lord Ashbourne, who bad come specially from Dublin that morning to attend. and who bad an interview with Sir Michael Dicks-Beach, at tbe Irish Secretary's residence previous to the meet- ing of the Cabineti under4tood that the principal_ business the Cabinet had to consider was the gliestioff ot strengthening the criminal law in Ireland. With regard to the Round Table Conference, writes the Leeds Mercurg London correspondent, all that can, be said is that, both Sir YiTilliam Harcourt and Mr. Chamberlain continue to be hopeful. Mr. Chamber- lain's letters and speeches, I am informed, differ very much from his tone in private. While publicly he is full of bitterness and venom, privately be is conciliatory' and moderate, and hence it is that the Conference stilt goes on. If the member for West Birmingham had. spoken at the Conference as he wrote to the Baptist. newspaper, the Conference would have broken up' long ago. Parliamentary returns issued on Saturday show that the total cost to candidates of the general election of 1886, amounted to £624,086, equal to 4s. per vote polled. In England and Wales the cost was £515,683, or 4s. DI. per vote polled, and included £109,051 'for returning, officers' • expenses. In Scotland, the cost was £82,858. or 4s. 7d. per vote polled, including £18,896 for returning officers' charges; and in Ireland the amount expended, was £25,544, or 2s. sd. per vote polled, including £12,988 for returning,_, officers' charges. The cheapest election was Mr. 'Richard Power's, Waterford City, £lO 10a., and the most expensive, Mr. Vernon's, South Ayrshire, £1,828. ,

A deputation representing the Sheffield Town Council waited on the Home Secretary, on Monday, to urge the desirability of a Royal Commission to inquire into the fraudulent use of trade marks. Mr. Mun&lla, introduced, the deputation, and stated they were' fully impressed, with the urgency for immediate legislation, but sooner, than have the GoVernment bill in its present shape they wished an. exhaustive inquiry with the view to iahowing what were the real evils to be rejeadied. The Govern- ment bill was unintelligible, and Would be unworkable.. Mr. Matthews said the Government were entirely at one with the deputation in wishing to strike at practices which injured English trade, but he thought they had sufficient information for the purpose of legislation. All the evidence that might be forwarded would be. weighed with the utmost care, but he felt that sooner than delay matters longer it would be better to legislate at once according t 6 their present lights. At a meeting of the Aberdeen Unionist Liberal Corn-, mittee on Monday a letter was read from Sir li. 0. Tre- velyan, replying to an invitation to visit Aberdeen. The requisition, he said, bore evident signs of being: exceptionally weighty and influential, and he was' was proud to have earned the confidence of such a.' body of men. His own view of the present situation was that the Irish question must be dealt with promptly and thoroughly—thoroughly, radically, and remedially— and it could only be so dealt with by a re-united Liberal party. The events of the last eight or nine mouths in Parliament and Ireland had conclusively shown that such was the case. For that reunion on terma. honourable to all concerned, he believed the moment to be ripe. The opinions on the practical points, of the problem held by leading Liberals, with. whom he was acquainteAl were such as, he was satis- fied, admit a their working together without any of them losing their respect for each other or themselves. If these were the views of those who had invited him to Aberdeen, he would try and make arrangements to come, though' it would not be very soon. The committee passed a resolutionothatiking Sir George for his letter. and asking him to come to Aberdeen during the present spring. The requisition was signed by 1,700 persons. Fr arenmenee sake he recognises the impor- tance and justice of the movement, but arges that the press- ing autY .01 himself and the Liberal party is to "clear the road" by the eettlement of the Irish qnestino. . Tinsley, William Sharp, John White, together with my son will have the kindness to take charge of the money, and as a committee devote it to the objects for which it is intended.—Yours faithfully, GILBERT GREENALL.

Robert Davies, Esq. This is all very good so far as the Church is concerned, and the clergy ought to be grate- ful; but, in the name of St. Helen and all the other Saints, what does Sir GILBERT mean by offering this as " a jubilee Gift to the 10Wfl of Warrington ?" It is a gift to a sect pure and simple; and, as one swallow does not make a summer, one sect does not make a town. Dr. MactKin was before Sir GILBERT in the way of a gift in the odour of sanctity ; he presented each policeman who accom- panied him to the Parish Church as the new Mayor with !s. Church Service; but we are not aware that this was offered as " a Jubilee gift to the town of Warrington." If the precedent which Sir GILBERT has set is to be followed we may have the CHIEF CONSTABLE presenting his wife with a new bonnet as "a jubilee gift to the town of Warrington." He might, of course, do worse, but from a public point of view he could hardly do anything that would be more likely to make Juhilee gifts look ridiculous. It might, we grant, he argued from the terms of Sir GILBERT'S letter that it is premature to conclude that he has in !hisraind the Establis- hed Church only, when he speaks of "further provision for divine service." We are not, to be sure, in his confidence, nor are we, it would seem, entitled to ordinary courtesy, for I the announcement of this Jubilee Gift was !mot sent to this journal—a circumstance in l'itself suggestive of its being intended fora :section only—but, going beyond this, we rmay say that we happen to know that the i.money is solely for Church purposes. The I Rev. W.. 11. PARRY, who is working hard in la poor district as the minister of Cockhedge IMission Chapel, read the lines of Sir Gin- BERT'S letter rather than what was between' the lines, and proceeded to test the value of! the "Jubilee gift to the town of Warrington" by applying to Mr. ROBERT DAVIES for par- ticulars of the scheme for the distribution of the fund. He soon had his eyes opened—if they were not already open—to the fact that there was no hope of a Dissenter being 'entrusted with a penny of the money. It might go in the direction of St. Peter's parish, Bank Quay, Bank-street, or Holy Trinity, but it must be "Church, Church, Church " at every step. The Rev. W. R. ! PARRY was thus in good time the means of settling the main point; and he came awayl wiser than he went in another respect, for he learnt that the gift must not be looked upon ! as political, as it was not the intention of Sir GILBERT to present himself as a candidate at the next !election, It would seem, therefore, ! that- the aged baronet intends the £5,000 as ' his " footing!" to the Peerage. He does not count on any slip between the cup and the lip; and we hope there will be none, for we can all rejoice—gift or no gift—at the pros- pect of !ceasing to represent Warrington, by being removed to that Hospital for; Decayed Politicians which is commonly known as the House of Lords. THE Corporation of the City of London is the greatest Corporation in the world, and if the charges -which were brought against it in ! the House of Commons on Tuesday are well founded it would seem also to be the most ' corrupt. There was an attempt made to re- form the Corporation whee Mr. GLADSTONE was in office in 188+, and Sir WILLIAM HAR- COURT thad Charge of a bill upon the subject. I It will be remembered that metropolitan ' Liberals had a strong feeling as to the need of reform, and that they even went the length, at the Leeds Conference, of,pressing the matter as of equal importance to the question of extending the county franchise. ; They knew that they were helpless and in ! the hands of the City Corporation.; and they ' knew, too, that money was at that time being improperly spent in order to raise up a bogus opposition to the Government measure. ' Reports appeared in the papers of mysterious meetings said to have been held by various ! classes of citizens who were opposed to the bill. It was found that gangs of ruffians stormed and tried to break up peaceable , meetings held in the usual way to demand the • reform of the City Government. It was rumoured at the time that the Corporation , furnished the funds for the hire of these dis- turbers of the peace; but the report seemed ' so incredible that it received but little atten- tion. Corruption of this kind, however, like murder, mill out: and on Tuesday night Mr.l GEORGE HOWELL, who has been patiently . and carefully investigating the matter, ' had a terrible tale to tell of what ! looks like misappropriation and corrupt ! use of pnblic funds. From an examination ! of the Corporate accounts, he found that in one year as much as £15,000 had been spent I for the manufacture of fictitious public opin- ion. In connection with a bogus meeting, held at Battersea, there were items in the 1 accounts of Luz for committee, Li los for stewards. and £ 5 for " hire of attendance to ' compose the meeting." Aso called Confer- ence of London Democrats was found to I consist of Eve persons only. and the cost was £6 IS. compared with this, the Conference of West London delegates was quite an irn ' posing demonstration; for there were as , many as thirteen persons present who, if ; they hadn't much to say, seeni to have had a , deal to drink. Mr. PETERS, who was ad- dressed in a letter by Lord ALISRURY as "My Dear PETERS," presided over this ! assembly, which was held in the Montpelier Tavern. Anotheu meeting, in which Lord , GEORGE HAMELTON took part, cost as much !as £195 s Bd. The House of Commons , seems to have been highly amused with the ;extraordinary details of this extraordinary expenditure; but it Seems to US to be a matter ' rather for indignation than hilarity. Sir R. N. FOWLER, one of the city members, and a member, too, of the committee \at which these charges are levelled, professed to treat this matter as one of " anonymous tittle-tattle," upon which Mr. B RaDLAuGH. justly angry, pointed out that Sir ROBERT had not even denied the accuracy of the charges. He went on to say that if an in quiry were granted, with power to examine witnesses on oath, he would " undertake to connect the hon baronet for the city of London with the issue of city funds under conditions which compel knowledge on his part. that they were corruptly used ;" and he added that he would prove his statements up to the hilt. Mr. LABOUCHERE said if a name was wanted he would give his own; he would make him- self- responsible for the "tittle-tattle." He had official letters and books to prove what had been stated, and would produce them if an inquiry were granted. Lord GEORGE -1-lasnizosr sought to throw dust in the eyes of the House by suggesting that there should be an inquiry, too, into the proceedings of I the Municipal Reform League Association ; but Mr. GLADSTONE, who treated the•whole question as one—to use his own words—of

"extreme gravity," pointed out that the issue was not as to whether there had been an attempt either on one side or the other to manufacture public opinion;, but whether there was ground for Mr. HOWELL'S conten- tion that "public funds had been used by a public body for a purpose which was un- doubtedly illegitimate and apparently corrupt." He urged that an investigation should be in- stituted; and there was nothing for it on the part of the Government but compliance or ignominy. There will therefore be an in- quiry; it will be one doubtless of a most searching character; and, if so, we infer from the foretaste that it will reveal a mass of cor- ruption under which the City Corporation will eventually dEsappear, to make way for a representative institution which will be more in harmony with the spirit of the age.

-- LACROSSIC.—WIDNES V. SOLITIIPORT.—Tbede clubs met at Southport on Saturday for the return fixture. The weather WAS fine, but windy, and the grourad WAS in splendid order. Neither club was well represented, the Widnes captain (F. W. Gossage), and Sayce being away from the visitors' ranks, while Southport were without the services of Norris and Richardson. Despite the fact that Widnes were playing 13. men to their opponents' 12, they immediately took the lead, scoring 4 goals to 1 before half-time. Wi h the wind in their favour, Southport pressed the visitor's almost the whole time, but, owing to the -good defence of the Widnes men, only two more goals were scored. SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE GOOD TEMPLAR'S: AN- NUAL Szssres.--J he annual session of the South- West Lancashire District Lodge of Good Templara was held on Monday at the Albert Hall, Liverpool. The' odge was opened by Brother J. W. Hall, of Warrington, D.C.T., and the whole of the officers were present. Several visitors from other districts occupied seats on the platform. The reports of the various officers were read, that of the D.C.T. being of a very interesting chdracter. Brother Hall re- ported upon the position of the various lodges, and pointed out what steps should be taken to improve their numbers. The District Secretary (Brother Morris Jones) repurted, in tabulated form, the several gains and losses in the various lodges in the district, and urged upon the members to renew their energies to make the Good Templar Order more powerfully felt in the Jubilee year. The D.E.S. (Brother J. Pickersgill), in his reportrcalled attention to the expenditure for intoxicating liquorsin our workhouses. He also dealt with the question of the united temperance bodies forming a separate and distinct party, to bring forward for boards of guardians, town councillors, and mem- bers of Parliament men of prohibition views. Brother It. Anders (S.J.T.) reported that the mem- bers of the Juvenile Temples limbered 1,510;an in- crease of 72 compared with the last report. The next business was the election of five representatives
of the District Lodge to the Grand Lodge Session at London in Easter week. The following gentlemen
were elected :—Brothers M. Jones IL. W. Williams. _ .

_ and R. W. Kirkus, of 19iverpol J. W. Hall, of Warrington; and George (larke, of Earlestown. The election of officers for the ensuing year resulted as follows :—D.C.T., Brother J. E. div.p: .'TOUCH AND GO."

'On Tuesday the Bishop of Liverpool swore and subscribed the roll." This sounds very shocking—particularly when one is re- minded of the injunction—'' Swear not at all." But Bishops are, perhaps, like troopers—they may be privileged as to "swearing:'

That piece of " stupendous dampness"— as the Yankee poet called the Falls of Niagara—is about to be made to do its duty. It is stated that an English syndicate has secured a charter for utilising the water power for manufacturing and electric light- ing purposes. We hope it will succeed, for we ourselves are thinking 'of obtaining a charter to utilise the hot springs of Iceland for the world's washing.

Measles, from which a large number of children in Warrington have been suffering, has been imported from Germany to Stony- hurst College. and there have been four deaths amongst the students. People cannot be too particular in taking precaution against infection. The disease in this case has spread to the children of the adjoining vil- lage (Hurst Green), and the schools have had to be closed.

Mrs. Mackey, the matron of the Warrtng- ton Workhouse, is amply justified in demand- ing that the Board of Guardians and the Local Government Board should explain themselves in the step they are taking to ap- point another Matron because her husband, the Master, has resigned. If it is "the law," she must submit; but in that case she must be parted with as one whose long and honourable services are fully and fairly re- cognised.

The session is not yet two months old, and already Liberal Unionists are showing signs of haying had enough of Tory incapacity. Lord Lymington expresses himself as unable any longer to remain silent at "the want of action, of nerve, and of courage which is paralysing the Government treatment of the Irish question." He thinks a policy "of fumbling lawyers and confused officials will disgust English gentlemen and the English public "—and he is right. Mr. Goschen as Chancellor of the Ex- chequer is not to be wheedled into taking off the carriage tax. A deputation, on Tuesday, told him a pitiful tale of the falling off of orders and of the great number of second- hand carriages on hand—due, they said, to the deprecsing effects of the tax. Mr. Goschen saw the facts in another way, and gently suggested that what they were suffer- ing from was a common complaint—depres- sion of trade. Still, a* to second-hand car- riages, he was a little puzzled; he thought people must be buying new as the old ones got out of Cashion. The deputation did not score, but Mr. Goschen did.

Mr. Raikes, too, is distinguishing himself. As things go he will soon have the reputation for being the worst Postmaster-General that the service has known. It is one of the curses of the United States that postal appointments are given to political favourites, and Mr. Raikes is following this bad example. He lost the last election in Liverpool, so the Tories say, by the mull he made of it in the matter of the mail contracts. Now, if he will only keep on and "keep it up," he will do the work of two or three men in helping to overthrow the Government.

The disclosures which are being made as to the corrupt practices of the London Cor- poration will doubtless cause Lord Salisbury to wish he had been a little less attached to the man whom he once addressed as " My Dear Peters." It is said that some of the damaging documents, which Mr. Labouchere keeps in a "burglar proof safe," were ob- tained in a seizure for rent at the offices of the Ratepayers' Association, and others were given up by a repentant and needy clerk, What coincidence, and in the nick of time! It is as good as a play. The following " tit-bits " as to the late Bishop Fraser's popularity in Lancashire, are from the " Life of Bishop Fraser," by Mr. Thomas Hughes, which is just published "A sturdy Dissenting operative waited for him at the bottom of the stairs after one of his earliest meetings, and scized him by the hand, with the remark, • Ah, bishop, thou'd'st mak' a foine Methody preacher.' Another, waiting for him outside church atter a charity sermon, forced a sovereign into his 'hand with, • Bishop, here's a pound for thee.' Bishop: Thanks, my friend, for the charity.' Operative, ' Nay, nay—for thysel.' "

A considerable number of people have been fined in the St. Helens and Prescot district for hav'ing neglected to take out dog licences in time. Amongst others fined was Mr. Thomas Pilkington, J.P., though Mr. Swift, so:icitor, stated in his behalf that his client had depended, as usual, on .the printed reminder from the Excise authorities, which II had not been sent. Singular to say, it was proved that in one case a reminder had been sent to another gentleman (rj?ei the date for , which Mr. Pilltington was summoned. This system of making; fish of one and flesh of another is intolerable : it brings the law into contempt. The rule should be to send ,a notice to all who have previously paid for dogs, or to none at all.

THE JUBILEE. The Chairman said as they were no doubt all aware the Duke of Westminster bat been empowered by the Prince of Wale t.) take the matter of the Impelial Institute into con. eideration as far RS the county of Cto-ster was concerned, I 1 and a large c9minittee had been formed to Fes what could be done. He (the Chairman) had been placed upon the committee, and if any gentlemen felt inclined to support the Imperial Institute he should be very glad to receive Rah-. scriptons and forward them on to the treasurer through the Dake of Westminster. With regard to the local celebration of the Jubilee, he suggested that a public Meeting should be called at an early date to discuss in what manner they would perpetuate the memory of the Queen, whose life had been as perfect ask was possible for a life to be. This was all the business.

div.p: A JUBILEE' RHYMN FOR WARRING-

TON. Neaw then, folk, wod abeawt this Jubilee? Come, speyk yer minds an' say wod hes 't to be? Ther'll be, of course, a underlie big processun - (Ther ales is to mark Owd Time's progressun) Banners an' bands, yo' know, an' tootle- turns, Full tilt vi "See the conquering hero comes." Will 't works stop? Really, neaw Wod am aw saying— • Heaw could fooak tee to work when th' bands wear playin' ? Wotus use o' th' Queen—wot's use o' th' Jubilee, If them as wants korn'd hey a bit of a spree? Fuddle an' feed, my lads, when yo' get th' chance, And if yo'r legs is bee, set to an' dance; Grab wod comes in yo'r way—dornd cry for th moon; An' be content at last—to watch th' balloon

• LAn' is this to be e'? Shall there nod be Something moor worthy of a Jubilee? ; Something a Queen might hear on 'ay, an' say-- "They blessed themselves in blessing me that day.* Eawr Queen likes books; hr husband liked 'em too, For eh, he knew hissel wod gov.l they do. Then wheer's a better thing for 1:1' Jubilee Than mekin th' Public Library fi•oo Let young an' ovad hey books to set 'era thinking—. Better th' end than bein' led oil to drinking. Just th' picture th' lads and lasses fresh fro' th' skoo— Skittish an' wild scarce knowing wod to do Yo' know wed traps is set to mA 'em roam— Then offer better bait to stop at home; (live 'em free range o' books, an' let 'em find Ther's such a thing as pleasure for the mind; Pleasure that needn't mek 'em hing ther head; Pleasure that lives when other joys are dead. . Id kom'd be done, yo say ? nay dornd say thad ; Eiwr situation is n'd varra bad. Ther's twenty theasand books upon yon' shelves, An' th' teawnsfolk owt to have 'em to therselves ; Bought eawt o' th' rates, id's a gre't shame indeed That but a few should tek 'em home to read. Nob'ry's a reet to charge, wode'er id be, When th law says plainly as id shall be "free,"' "Fair play's a jewel —th' brightest jewel th' Queen, Empress, or Emperor has ever seen; I Then let it glitter at this Jubilee By reeking th* Library really Free.

ACT AT WIDNES.

On Thursday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, Mrs. Sarah Ellen Lomax, keeper of the Sun Inn, Victoria" road, was charge.l with having allowed intoxicating liquors to be consumed on the premises daring pro- hibited hdurs. Mr. J. 0.• Swift defended. At twenty minutes to twelve on Sunday. the 20th February, Sergeants Robinson and McGregor saw a man named Thompson leave the defendant's house by the front door, and upon searching him found a quart of beer in his possession. Thompson stated the liquor was given to him by Mrs. Lomax for cleaning the house, and the officers, entering the house to ascertain the correctness of his story, saw two young men named John Williams and Henry Gillow leaving by the back door. There was ti 1 glass of freshly drawn beer on the table, and also a bottle, but the landlady removed these before the sergeants could get to them. The defence was that Thompson had the beer given to him for clean- ing; that Williams was a lodger, and that Gillow had only entered the house to ask him to go a walk. The glass of beer, Mr. Swift argued, only existed in I the imagination of the officers. The Bendh did not 1 consider that a printa,faeis case had been made out, and dismissed the charge. William Bailey Cross, landlord of the Royal Oak Inn, Catherine-street, was summoned under two in- formations charging him with having kept open during prohibited hours, and with allowing intoxi- cating liquors to be consumed during prohibited hours.—James Whelan, 37, Lacey-street, James Con- cannon, Widnes-road, and Joseph Hunt, Bent-sti cct, wer charged with being on the premises during e\ prohibited hours. Mr. Swift defended. At about 1 twenty minutes to eleven on Sunday night, the 6th February, P.S. Strickland, with Constables Porter .and Davey, seeing a light in the bar parlour of the Royal Oak, and hearing the jingling of money on the counter, knocked at the door' and after L three minutes, delay were admitted. There were four other men besides the defendants in the parlour, and there were a number of beer and spirit glasses on the table. Whelan was drank and two other men who came from Warrington also "appeared 'to be drunk. After hearing the evi-, dence for the defence, the Bench dismissed the charge of keeping the house open, and tined Cross £2 and costs on the second information. Superin- . tentlent Barker withdrew the ,case againAt if, int, and the 13mch dismissed the charge against Con- cannon, and lined Whelan lOs and costs.

WiItRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. The monthly meeting of thief:lmam:U.-was held in the Council Chamber on Tuesday evening. Tnere were present the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere), Aldermen Bargefet, Sutton, Cbandley, Holmes, and Webster; Councillors Greening. Brown, Jolley, Platt, Barker, Greene', Dixon, Dakin, F. A. Roberts, Bolton, J. Pierpoint. Tinsley. Heaton, Litton, H Roberts, Wright, Marsh, Franoonab, Fleming, Taylor, Hutchinson; Mews'. Bronk (town clerk), Whittle (deputy town clerk). Chorley (borough treasurer), and Paterson 1 (gsa manager). THE NORTH-EAST WARD. With regard to this election, the Towx CLEsts reported the return of Mr. Frank A. Roberts as a councillor of the North-Etst Ward. (Hear, hear.) EtEcTlitu AUDITORS. The Tows CLERK. also read the return of the election of Mr. John Harrison and Mr. J L. Tunstall as elective audi- tors of the Borough, ad the appointment of Mr. Councillor Brown as the Mayo's auditor for the Borough. THE LATE MR. W kRRINGToN WOOD. The following letter WM received:—" Would you kindly convey to the members of the Town Council my feelings of thanks and gratitude for their kind expressions of sympathy awl condolence on the over-whelming affimtion that has no suddenly befallen me in the death of my loving, devoted and only son, J. Warrington Wood, and how rnuca I value the tribute so kindly paid to his Heats and memory.—Most respectfully yours, Charlotte Wood." A MEMORIAL OF THE FRIARY. The MAYOR maid there had been some correspondence be- tween Mr. James Nicholson, of Tioilwall, and Mr. B.amont, with reference to the old Friary site in. Bridge-street. He had also had a lever from Mr. Nicholson, suggesting that the Corporation should place a tablet with an inscription on the site of theold Friars Gate, that was the plot of land opposite Mrs. Bowes' school. The cost would be very little, and he intended to bring the matter forward at the • =mango( the General Purposes Committee. C(1121101.11. JOHN Piegroner said that pehhape Mr. Nic- .holson and ens or two antiquarians would pay the cost of. the tablet. The MAYOR : I should be sorry to ask them, Mr. Pier- point. I think it is as little as we can do, because it would be a memorial of what has been, and if the Corporation can't all ird a few shillings it would he a shame to aak any- one elso to do it.

The minutes of this committee contained as follows "6 Resolution OW the nurcher of carritges authorised to Jetted on the stand in Wirmick-straet opposite to the en- trances to the Central Railway Station be reduced to threz. and that a stand for four carriages be approved in Crown- street." On the motion of the MAYOIt, sPconded by Alderman Cuernor.ev, the minatei were confirmed. FINANCE . .

Alderm in HOLINF.S, in m—o-vin-i-the confirmation of the rill:wee of the Finance Committee,which contained nothing of importace,sai i that at a meeting of the committee on the previoue day, a recommendation RaS matte that the eatiniates of the, committee should be prepared yearly 19eread of half. yearly asheretofore. They believed Out it wohld save a lot of tAinur. Toe minutes were conarmed. STREET IMPROVEMENT AND LIGHTING COMMITTEE. ADOPTION OF PLANS.

At a rneeting of the Sweet Improvement and Lightinr Committee it was resolved that a plot of land containing inl vinare yards. in Thel wall-lane, Latchford. be purchased Of NE, Joseph Hell, at 5e per yard, for the purpose of im- provirlie and widening Thelwall-laue; and that Councillor Platt be elected the chairman, and Councillor Greening the deputy-chairman of this committee for the rem under of the year--it lets rreommended that the following pl ens be ap- proved :—Plan of iron abed in Sankey-street for Messrs Williams and Clay; of additions to brier/ell near Dillam: tine for Messrs P. Waker and inn ; of fur cottages in Upnerel-street, for Mr. J. Wilding ; of Airo.ir,idnis to oil club ill Academy-street, for the Otserver Co , Limited ; and pi at of two cottages in Latchford. for Messrs Par- itinpon. Councillor PLAirr moved the confirm-Jinn of the minutes. Alluding to the purchase of land in faa,chford, he ohaerved that it wes at the point of Theierall.lane ni-arrst to Warring- •ton. It WAS an improvement which hid been want.d a long time. When Mr. Vawser was the Berouzh Surveyor an attempt fri-.9 ide to purchase the and, end th*e oiler then made was the same as th tntme nom which they were now -able Co secure the land. (hoar, hear.) Councillor MIMIC seconded the mlootion of the minutes, which was agrred to. UNITARY COMMITTEE —GRATUITY OF' £lOO TO TICE BOROUGH SITSVETOB.

Tilt. Sanitary COOlusittme rn. t on the 9th February, when Nveg resolvoil that the Council be recommended to you to Mr. Lonudiofthe bmougb surveyor, the sem of £lOO as a gratuity for the extra services rendered hi ties in connec- tion with the erection of the interceptinit &pots and the ex- tenons At Longfed The resolution w,is passed °minim- *ltaly at ft full meeting, every member of the committee bjog, present. It was resolved that the reconvnendatlon be submitted tn the G.,nersi Purposes Committee f.r their ap- proval and support —A eepy of the order recoiling dogs to be muzzled in the borough during March waa also given in -the misleads.

Alderman BURGESS, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said the order respecting dogs had been made in consEquence of information given by one of the veterinary inspectors, upon which they were bound to act. The re- commendaiion 'that a gratuity of £lOO be given to Mr. Loogdin was adopted at a full 3nd unanimous meeting of the committee, and, in venturing to ask the Council to give its confirmation, be did so in the full confidence that they would have the general support of the Council. The reason of the re- cammendation was that Mr. Longdin, as borough surveyor, undertqok the carrying out of a work that the Council placed upon him. and he had carried it out in a very matt. trly manner. They did net ask that there should be an advance in his salary, but at the same time they knew that the amount they proposed to give did not pay for the over- titne that he had had to give to the Council during the last twelve mouths. Besides that, the nature of his duties had been most disagreeable, and he knew that in consequence Mr. Longdin's health had suffered. Alderman SurroN seconded the motion.

Councillor Purr moved as an—a-m-e-n-dment to the pro- posal that the recommendation that £lOO be paid to Mr. Longdin be not conSrmed. His chief reason for doing so was that he thought Mr. Longdin was exceedingly well paid already. (Hear, bear.) Mr. Longdin was appointed on the 9tk January, 1878, at a salary of £250 a year. In February, 1879, his stlary was advanced to £3OO, and at the same time he received a bonus of £5O, which be sup- posed was for special services, but still services which came within the scope of his duties, as be expected did the ser-1 vices On the present occasion. In 1880 his salary was in- creased to £4OO. He thought everybody would say that this was a very rapid increase, and he thought that Mr.Longdin for a borough of the size of Warrington was being exceed- ingly well paid. He had no means of knowing what the "special services" were which Mr. Longdin had rendered, but he thought it must be admitted that if he had been giving the whole of his time to the Sanitary Committee the work ef other committees had suffered in consequence. (Hear, heat ) He (Mr. Platt) did not think that Longford itself had been any great source of credit either to Mr.Long- din or the Sanitary Committee. An encemous amount of money bad been spent, but they could not say yet that the money had been well spent, as the work was only in an ex- perimental stage. They could not tell yet whether the Longford works would pay, or whether they would merely prove a costly Oxperiment and he objected to paying auy gratuity on that ground. (Hear, hear.) . .

ICouncillor BARER secOnded the Motion. At the same time he wished to know whether the chairman of the Sanitary Committee would supply him with the infor- mation for which he asked at the lest meeting of the Council.

Alderman BURGES3 said that, with the permission of the Council, he would give the reqeired information. Coun- cillor Barker asked five questions. The first question was: What quantity of excreta and ashes were taken to the depot daring the past three months? The anawerwas : From November 20th to February 17th, secrete, 1,492 tons. 19 cwt.; ashes, 2,770 tons, 3 cwt., 1 qr. 2. How muck of this has been passad through the machinery? The whole. 3. What quantity of concentrated manure was manufactured In the three months? 92 tons, 10 cwt. 4. What number of hours the machinery has worked to produce this given weight of manure? General work, 1,560 hours, vacuum pans, 1,383 hours. The fifth question is : And what amount of wages has been paid in the three months to produce this Quantity? £255 1586 d, including manager's salary. Alder- man Burgess observed that he hoped Councillor Barker would renew his questions at the end of 12 months, when the results of their workiug would be in a more complete form. (Hear, hear.) COUNCILLOR BOLTON supported the amendment. He was opposed to gratuities altogether, as he thought they were I wrong. They were simply premiums upon experiments, for I • deny official got up a fad and had it carried out be would be paid a premium when the thing nes done. They could not afford to raise salaries at the present time, and he re- garded the money of the ratepayers in the same light as he would hold in trust the money of a poor family who did I not know where the nest was coaling frilk (Hear, hear). He pointed out that Mr. Longdin beside asal cry of £409 had assistants in his office one of whom got £l5O a year and I altogether they werespending about £7OO a year in the isarveyor's department. The extra service& they were asked to vote for were not defined in any way. He pected that the next thing they would have would be the Sanitary committee asking them to vote .£lOO to each mem- ber all round. (Laughter, and hear, hear). There were ten of them on that Committee and they bad gone to the General Parposea Committee and told a smooth tale with the result that it was simply a fiasco bringing the matter forward at the Council at all, for if 19 of the members of the Council had already agreed to the resolution what WAS I the use of asking the other sixteen. (Hear, heard He also remarked that it was not the members of the Council who directly represented the ratepayers that were most eager to pass that resolution. (Hear, hear.) Councillor bare PIERPOINT opposed the proposal and urged that for the present they ehonid let the matter remain where it was, and in coarse of time, when they saw that everything was a semen appertaining to the machinery at Longford depot, let the matter be reconsidered, and the greater credit would be due to the chairman of the Sanitary. Committee, and to those who had aseisted by their energy and ability I as Mr. Longdin had done. (Hear, hear.) Councillor Measit supported the proposal of the commit- tee and expressed the hope that they might long retein the services of so valuable a gentleman as Mr. Longdin. (Hear, hear.) • Alderman Surroer said that if they had not had the ser- vices of Mr. Longdin they would have been compelled to have employed some other surveyor, equally clever, and have paid him three or four times as much as they were now paying Mr. Longdin. Alderman CHANDLEY thought that a cheeseparing policy was the way to snub ell ambition in a servant The bor- ough surveyor bad every right at a certain hour to lock his door and go home. Mr. Lobgdin had not 610ne so, but had done what they might call works of supererogation. He contended that £lOO was a very poor reward for the work he had done for Longford alone. (Heer.hear.) Councillor JOLLEY said Mr. Longdin had rendered many services outside his ordinary routine work, and if he bad been a mechanic he would have received so much per hour for overwork. Seeing that the work had been done, he did not see how they could in fairness refuse to allow the amount , proposed. . .

COUNCILLOR Dtxox argued that there hid been no nec- essity for extra service on the part of the Borough Surveyor at Longford. COUNCILLOR H. ROBERTS said that he believed that it was their duty as the representatives of the ratepayers to act as honest stewards ever the money entrusted to their care. There was such a thing as false economy: They might have a servant who performed his duties in merely a perfunctory manner, and they might be badly off in conse- (pence ; and, on the other hand, they might have a servant who threw the whole et his energies into the performance of his duty, and they could not treat that eervent too well. (Hear, bear.) Mr. Longdin had given to the important question to which reference had been made considerably more time and energy than his agreement with the corpora- tion required him to do. He did not agree with the suggestion that had been made, that if the seanitary question had been a failure it would !ewe rested upon the Committee. 'He members of the council seemed to forget that the Borou4h Surveyor had a reputation at stake, and if his work had been a failure his reputation and position would have been I blasted very likely for life. On the contrary, however, the I work was a success ("No, no,") and it was an undoubted fact that as regarded the collection of the refuse itself they were saying the town £1,500 a year. He supported the re- solution simply because if, as an employer of labour, he put ' a servant to do a certain work, and he had to work beyond his ordinary hours, considerably beyond them, whether that particular work sueceeded or not, be should feel in common , honesty bound to make some recompense for the extra labour and anxiety involved in carrying out his request (Hear, hear.) Alderman HOLmE9 supported the resolution, and re- marked that Mr. Longdin was fully entitled to the payment it was proposed to mike to him. It had been frequently said that the rates of the town were high ; but taking all I the rates into consideration, they were this year only 5e Bd, which was Les than usual, although there had been an ex- pensive lot of work done, including sewerage alterations, &c. The expenditure during the year had been increased, but the town had been able to pay it. owing to the increased assessment of the town. The alderman read some ex- tracts from a return, showing the assessable 4ealoe and ,rates levied from the year 1857 to 1888. In 1857 the assessable value was £54,321, and in 1888 £129,898. .

Councillor oREEKI. NG. in supporting the resolution, eat& that he had always found it advisable to pi', a an for the eztra services he had rendered. Alderman BURGESS then replied on the discussion. He complained of the vicious and acrid tone in which he said Councillor Platt had addressed his ohservations to the Council, and Councillor PLevr appealed to be protected against ill•natnred and vicious remarks like thoee need by the alderman. Proceeding, Alderman Burgess replied at length on the arguments used in favour of the amend- ment.

On the amendment being submitted, the following voted for it :—Councillore John Pierpoint, Platt, Heaton, Bolton, Barker, Dixon, and Oreenall-7. The followinrr voted against the amendment :—The Mayor, Aldermen Webete.r, Sutton, Harrison, Holmes, Burgess, and Chandlev ; Coun- cillors Tinsley, Francomb, J. V. Taylor Wriglit, Brown, Jolley, Greening, Hutchinson, Marsh, ii. Roberts, Litton, F. Roberts, Dakin-20. The amendment was, therefore, low. • The minutes were then adopted, PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMbfITTEE. This committee recommended the adoption of various tenders, and Submitted a report of the borough surveyor in regard to the sewer in Dial-street, in which it WAS recom- mended that the sewer should be taken no, and a 9.inch Dins sewer laid in its place, the estimated cast being about £5O. Councillor WRiairr proposed, and Councillor HUTCHIN• SON seconded, the confirmation of the minutes Councillor H. ROBERTS asked whether it Was the inten- tion of the committee to continue to give the twice of ten- ders. Personally he had nothing to say against it, but be thought it would be more consistent if the prices of all tenders were given. Alderman Smarms : If the Corporation desire to have. the particulars of the contracts, the committee will give them. The Mayon suggested that Councillor Roberts might enter a resolution to that effect tor consideration at the next meeting.

Councillor WRIGHT, replying to Councillor Bolton, said that the old sewer in Dial-street WA, nothing more or less than an elongated cesspool. The borough surveyor assured the committee that the proposed pipe would be quite suffi- cient.
The minutes were then passed. ECNOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE. _. .

This committee met on the 1-7-th-F-Zr-u-aTy, when tb. inspector reported that 111 cases had been inqaired into by the Board of Guardians' and school fees ;Wowed in 106 cases for 228 children, that 14 cases had been taken before tie magistrates, and fines inflicted in 11 cases. 1 ordered to the Workhome, 1 ordered to the ship Clio, and 1 adjourned. Thirty-one cases were brought before the committee and dealt with.
The minutes were c2nfirmed on the motion of Alderman Wnns-rEa, seconded by Councillsr Drams.

MUSEUM, LIBRARY, AND ARTS COMMITTEE. The report of the curator to this committee for the month of January was as follows :—Visitors to the Museum, 4,061 (partly closed January, 1886). • The Earlestown and Golborne teems again met on Satur- day afternoon on the ground of the llayclock Football Club, to decide who should have the honour of playing the Hay- dock Club in the final tie of the Wigan and District Asso- ciation Ckatinge Cup , Competition. The same teams met on the preeious Saturday, whey after a most exciting game the result was declared A draw of three goals each. 'The second meeting of the teams excited increased interest throughout the district, and there was a larger attendance than on the former occasion. It was estimated, that over 3,000 spectators were present. There was only one altera- tion in the two elevens. Wballev (Eulestown) sustained a severe injury to his ankle in the first match, and Ibis ren- dered him unable to play lest Saturday, and his place at half back was filled byJ Howard, of the second eleven, who played remarkably well t hroughoet the game. The teams turned out as follows :—Eerlestown : J Appleton, goal ; R Green (captain) and G Clough. backs ; J W Sims, J Green, and J Howard, half backs ; J Ellison and J Ogden, right wirg ; T Siddeley, centre; J Shaw and W Shew' left wing. The umpires were Messrs. Thompson, Westhoughton : and Rudd, Adlington ; and the referee Mr T Norris, of Bolton. Earlestown won the toss and elected to play uphill with the sun slightly in their favour. Flynn started the leather for Golberne and after some lose play in the centre of the field, the backs of both teams were called upon to defend their respective goals. A run down the field by tee Gol- borne left wing and in attack on the Earlestown goal ended in Lowe shooting the ball outside the posts. " Jimmy " Shaw and Ellison made a good run up the field, and a capital centre by the former enabled Siddeley to send in a stinging shot. which Jeokinson had a difficulty in defeating, ' near the corner of the goal. An exciting scrimmage fol- lowed, and straight shots for go-el from Sime, J Shaw, and Siddeley were repelled by Waddiagton, Clarke, and the goalkeeper, and to defeat the pers.stent attack on the goal Clarke kicked the leather into touch. The Eerlestonians shortly afterwards obtained•another corner, and from this a scrimmage ensued, and Siddeley sent the ball between the posts amid loud cheers, but the point was disallowed no a claire of "hands" Succeeding this was exciting ploy in close proximity to the Golborne nprighte, in which the bro- ther& Shaw and Siddeley made good attempts to score, but • they were unsucceseful until 30•m1nutes from the start, when J Shaw literally "brought down the house " by run- ning round Davies and shooting the leather through the corner of the eoel—beyond reach of the keeper—a [magni- ficent goal. Siddeley restarted the game, but Flynn secured the bell, and making the beet run of the day drieblelthe lea• titer past Howard. Clough, and R Green, and ended by scor- ing a good point in a few seconds from the restart. ,This feat evoked enthusiastic cheers though the score was an unex- pected one by Mende, and foes alike. MR. PIERfT MAITONLM P ON . • -iliELA.no Under Lin auspices of, the Warrington Liberal Association an address • was given. on Wednesday evening, in Wycliffe Hall, by Mr; Pierce Mahoney, Nationalist member for Meath, arid assistant Land Commissioner ; subject;"lrelandV2 The chair was taken by Mr. J. Platt, J.P.,• and there were also on the platform,,besides Mr. Mahoney. the-Rev. Father Care Wand Cresnoillors F. A. Reberts,-• N. Roberts, and J. H.. Fleming.. The hall was crowded to the door by a numerous and enthusiastic gathering. The Cuentidsas said he was pleased tossee such a large meeting there that night. The Irish question Was the question of the hour, and until that was settled, as their mat leader, Mr. Gladstone—(loud applause)—had very well said; itwas almost useless to hope for further progress in useful reforms. The Liberal party wa.spractically agreed upon a great many measures of useful reform, but that one re- form and amendment of our rule in Ireland stood in the way. They should have' to disposer of that before-they could do. anything else. (Applause.) There was a great difference in the way in which the Liberal party wished to treat the Irish question and the way in which the Tory party wished to treat it. (Hear, hear.) The Tory party. wished' to 'continue the old exploded fallacy of trying .to rule Ireland by force, but the Liberal party had made up its mind that :ruling by force would not do any longer. (Hear, hear, and, applause.) • Of , course England was strong enough torule Ireland by-force, but they had the authority of one who' had been a 'lvery good Liberal in his time, that "force is , • no, remedy." (Applause.) The• proper way to find a solution of the Irish question was to, settle it on lines acceptable to the people: themselves. 'They must rule them as the Liberal party had always wished to do in deal- ing with its fellow-men by doing uhto them as we would they should do 'unto us; , (Applause.) They. must not treat the Irish as-a nation that was to be kept down, but' 'as fellow-citizens of' this great Empire, and as those to whom they, were prepared to extend 'the right hand of fellowship. (Applause.) They must treat the Irish as brothers, as they were, and' hope that after that question was settled they would be on their side. The' great bulk of the- Liberal party had been stigmatised by the, Tory party, and some of those who ,hsed to be in their ranka, as theseparatist party. But they were not a separatist party. (Hear,- hear; and loud applause.) The Liberal party in England, Scotland', and throughouOthel Empire had no' wish for separation; they did not believe for a moment that the measures which Mr. Gladstone had proposed, and which he would carry eventually if spared to thenv--(ap- plause)—would lead to separation in the slightest degree. (Applause.) They did not want the Irish- men agiunst them but with.them, and he thought if- that question could be settled on equitable terms, as the Liberal party-wished to settle, they would have the Irish with them as friends. (Applause.) ' He was glad to see in that day's paper a letter from Sir G.-0. Trevelyan, in which he-,showed a very strong disposition to re-unite himself with the main body of the Liberal party again. (Hear, hear, and ap- plause.) It showed that Liberals who had gone astray for a short time were anxious to get back to the fold. Wellithey would extend the right hand of fellowship to them—to 'Mr. Chamberlain, to Sir George Trevelyan, and to any other of those who are now dissenting,from Mr. Gladstone's course, but they should not settle with them at all either at a round table or any where else. by giving up what they believed to be right. (Hear, hear, and ap- plause,) He himself believed. thoroughly that' their great leader, Mr. Gladstone, was right in that as he had Proved himself right so many times before. (Ap- plause.) When the qUegtion was settled on his lines, ten years after it would be accepted by both Liberals and Tories., and the only wonder' will ~be that there should have been so much bother about it. (Loud applause.) • Mr. MA.HONEY, who was received with loud ap-, plause, said that as soon as.the Franchise Act was passed by Mr. Gladstone, he felt in h* own mind that the Irish question was practically sittled, and for this reason. He always had very considerable- faith in the integrity of ,the masses of the British people; he always had a considerable faith in their love of justice, and he believed that when the power came into their hands they would listen calmly to the case which they had to put before them, and that they would do them substantial justice. Now that belief had been already to a great extent borne out. It was not very long since the power was placed in the hands of the people; they had as yet scarcelrleanit ,to use that power billy, but what was the result of the Franchise Act? What Mr. . Gladstone had .termed a "truce of God." (Ap- plause.) It was his (Mr. Mahoney's) wish, his en- deavour, and the chief reaseri for his' being there thenight, to assist in a small way in turning that "truce of God" into a lasting and enduring peace. (Applause.) Mr. Gladstonolhad already pointed out the way in which he believed that this country can , do justice to Ireland without any danger to itself. That policy was placed heave the country at the 'last-general election, but the people did not confirm it. But they. did not confirm the opposite policy. The last election was- lost through ab- stention; it. was lost because there were a number of people who were unable to Make up_ their minds. '(Hear, hear;) He did not blame them for that. The question was brought before them , very suddenly, before they had a full opportunity of inquiring into the merits of the case,, and they-saw some of those whom they had been accustomed to look to in the past as leaders go against Mr.. Glad- stone. Therefore, he thought that under all the circumstances of the case the wonder was that the measure received as much Support as it did. (Hear, 'hear.) He thought it was very much to the' credit of the English people that they. supported the mea- sure to the extent that they did, and he thought it augured well kr the future. (Applause.). Perhaps the most worthless, of the objections that were made to Mr..Gladkone's policy was that which en- deavoured' to appeal to religious bigotry. (Hear, hear.) He was there that night as a' Protestant Irishman. (Applause.) He was a Protestant re- l' turned to .Parimaneist by a Roman Catholic constitu- ency at the last election. The parish priest acted as his election agent, and he was a living answer to . the calumny-that had been hurled ,at the head of his Roman. Catholic' fellow countrymen. (Loud ap- plause.). He had lived for many years in a part of the country where the populabion was purely. Roman • Catholic. There was not a Protestant living within a distance a three or four miles,. except one in his own emplay, and:-• he had never received anything but the greatest possible kindness at the hands or hisltoman Catho- lic fellow-countrymen. • He had never known a single in- stance in which they Sad shown religious intolerancs, but , he had known several remark Able instances in which they bad shown great hberalitv of spirit. (Applause.) In A neighbouring poor-law electoral division they had elect, tthe only Protestant residing * the division to represent ' them on the poor-law Board, aids quite recently thaitoman Catholic constituency of South ponegal returned to Partin- ' merit as its member the son GI a Protestant clereemau, • Mr. McNeil. (Applause.) The Tortes said their policy was one Crown, one Empire, and one i'arlhiment. Well, they all agreed in the policy of one Crown and one Einpire, tiat as to one Parliament that was absurd, because at the present moment within thia Empire there were ik existence twenty-three Parliaments. If they would say one Imperial Pnrliament then he would say they all agreed about that also. (Applause.) They did not want to interfere with'. the authority of thoirsperial Parliament; they only wanted it to confiee its attention to imperial affairs. They wanted in Ireland to be left to manage their own purely domestic affairs. (Applauss.) Referring to the new proce- dure rules, he said they were now taid that question Lin Parliament w-re now Only -to have that trine allotted to them which their importaoce deserved, and he asked them if that was to he the /roe to invigine how Much time woald be given to local grievances whicii were often the most pressing, and the greatest possible injustice was often,done by not attending to them. (Hear. hears) They were told by the Tories that the.prestat proposed reform would lead to separation, but.
