div.head: _MARKETS COMMITTEE.
div.p: _MARKETS COMMITTEE.

This committee had resolved tbat the ground at the north end of the new market shed be covered with concrete cement. The total income from all sources was reported to be £244 lfis 7d. A memorial was read from tenants of the Market Hall calling attention to the complaint laid before the committee through a deputation which waited on them a month ago. Unless the committee could meet their re- quest, or .suggested a more feasible plan, they should be compelled, though reluctantly, to quit their present hold- ings. The reduction of rent mentioned is not what they desired. They wanted a chance of doing a fair trade, which cannot be procured under the present arrangements. It was resolved that the centre of the Market Hall be appropriated to the sale of eggs, butter, cheese, and bacon, and that one month's notice be given to the tenants who occupy stalls in the New Market Shed for the sale of such commodities to remove te the Market Hall.

Alderman CHILNDLn, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, said that the committee came to the concfnslon that it was desirable to remove those persons who sold butter and eggs back to the market hall from the market shed. Since he came into the room he had received a letter Dom Mr. Arthur Browne, solicitor, who represent.d the persons proposed to be removed, requesting that the committee would postpone further action in the matter until they bed been hard. Inasmuch as the butchers had been heard, be- thought in common equity the Council were bound to hear the other side of the question. He, therefore, suggested' that the minutes of the committee be confirmed with the ex- ception of that part referring to removal of the tenants of the stalls from the market shed to the market hall.
Councillor LaTots seconded th confirmstion of the minutes as amended, and the motion was pissed.

SELLING BUTTE RINE AS BUTTER. Several shopkeepers were summoned to the War- rington Borough Court on Monday, at the instance of the Corporation, to answer complaints of their having sold butter which was not of the nature and quality demanded. A summons against Messrs. Lavirrenson and Ward, provision dealers, Winwick- street, who were represented by Mr. T. J. Peters, of Widnes, was first heard. James Allen Short, a clerk in the employ of the Corporation, went to de- fendant's shop and asked for a pound of tenpenny butter. The shopman cut it from a pile of butter which Was marked 10d, and after weighing it and wrapping the butter up, he delivered it to witness, who tendered Is, and received 2d change. Witness told the shopman that he intended to submit the butter for analysis, and was told that he would find the conditions on which the butter was sold on the inside of the paper on which it was wrapped. The analyst's certificate showed that the butter con- tained 85 per cent. of foreign fat. In defence, Mr. Peters contended that there was no offence, as the purchaser of the butter had the nature of the arti- cle sold brought under his notice at the time the sale was effected. It was an accident that the label was wrapped inside. The Mayor said there was no doubt Messrs. lawrenson and Ward protected them- selves, or tried to protect themselves, by using the labels, and it might be an accident on the part of the manager in putting the butter on the wrong side. He did not think it was a case for a large penalty. His Worship advised the defendfints to be more careful in future, and let the peo- ple know that they were buying butterine, and not butter. A fine of 10s and costs was imposed.--Th ' A. E. A. Lmittlf, grocer, St. James'-street, Latchford, ' was similarly summoned. A man named John Ash- croft went to the defendant's shop and asked for a pound of butter at 10d. He NM served by Mrs. smith, and informed her that he wanted the butter for analysis. Mrs. Smith replied, that it was good butter, and called her husband downstairs. When he appeared she said "Is this not gala butter r and defendant said "No, it's butterine." Defen- dant said it had been the custom to' place a label on the butterine to indicate what was its nature; but it had been washed off. Fined 108 and costs.— Messrs. Sexton Brothers, grocers, were similarly charged, mid were also ,tined 103 and costs.—John and Thomas Edwards, provision merchants, of 114, Whitechapel, Liverpool, were summoned for selling to John Ashcroft a pound of butter which was not of the quality demanded. The sale took place at the People's Stores, 9, Irlam-street, and after \Ash- croft had paid for the butter and told the manager that he intended to submit it for analysis, the latter

IJGBI RULES. ORFORD TRUE BLrES v. WALKER'S ASIATECRS 2ND.— This match vral plair-d on the ground of the latter on Sat- urday, and after a good and exciting game the Blues won by 1 goal 4 minors to 2 minors.

_ WIDNES V. AS.PULL.—These teams met at &mull on Sat- urday, when an exceedingly well-contested game was brought re a close eight minutes before the expiration of time owing to a fracas between some of the players, at which time the score stood—Widnes one try and two minors to Aerpull two minors. During the fiat belt Moult played with a strong wind in their favour, and gained bath points. These, however' wem not a true indicatioo of the game, as they were both deed balls and the result of long kicks, which were not even made at goal ; whilst Widoes had hard lines in not scoring on several oCCOSiOni. When a change ' of enda was effected the Aepullites were in high expectation on account of the boasted staying powers of their men ; but their fondest idol was doomed to fall. Widnes pressed hard and compelled their opponents to saie, and then some I splendid dribbling and passing by Hardman, Plampton, Smith, Kiddie, and Fogg culminated in Smith obtaining a try close to .the posts. Farrell, however, failed to add the major point. No sooner had the ball been returned into , play than Widnes again rushed it dawn to their opponents' line, and Farrell got over, but loot possession and Aspull ' tortehed down. Filkington returned with the ball, but did not kick, and Hardman prevented him from going beyond the quarter line. This led to an unseemly al. tercetion. and as the spectators ruebed into the field, the game closed as above stated. Both teams were fully represented. WARRINGTON (A. TEAM) V. EDGE HILL (INT.) This match was leyed at Edge Hill on Saturday iu beautiful weather. Edge Hill won the toss, and elected to play down I hill with the wind in tbeir favour. Ashurst kicked off for Warrington, and a good return was in ade, but Nevins got I hold and ran to centre, being brought down by Tearable. The Warrington ferwards beerier by Jones, Mole/mans, and Ashurst, dribbled the bell claw to the Edge Hill hue, and Bite picked up nicely and err-emote/1 the hell over the line. I B iardman Was sacceedul at the puce kick. Ililtocr kicked ! off, and the vieitiret forwards took play to thT home quar- ters. Middleton relievel by a good run, and was brought down by Boirdrain. Williams trent punted to Boardman, who responded by a short run and kick into touch—Hac- kett, Eyes, and Dillon were next conspicuous with re lis'ae dribble, and Adenoma from a line out took play to the home line, Jones succeeding in getting over, but the point was disallowed.. Edge Hilt shortly afterwards were compelled to touch down.. Hilton dropped out, play far a time being in neutral groaod, when Bate got posseswon from the scrim- mage and peeled to Belebew, who transferred the oval to Boardman. CM latter player made a grand ran, but we, collared by Williams within a few plea of the line. Midue dleton and Berme relieved their lines by short kicks to ' touch, but Dillon, Jones, Adamson, and rtolvneanx again took the ball to the horns lines, Hilton again being forced to touch down. Shortly after the drop out Antrobus and Bete were Inse-urnental in working the ball into the Edge Hill 25, where Belehaar passed to Nevins, who almost got over. Half-time was now called the score standing: Warrington one goal and two minors to idge Hill nothing. On resuming, Morley kicked off for' Edge Hill, Uasworth inakina a good return. Aehurst and Jones broke away with a dribble, H I ton frgstrating their efforts by punting up the field. Jones obtained a free kick, the ball baing returned into touch. Dillon next came through the scrimmage with the bill, and Uasworth, following up well, almost gor over, a five var te' scrimmage being formed. Morley and McGrechin afforded temporary relief, but a pass by Antrohos to Nevins enabled that player to get in a short run and kick, the ball going dead. Hilton dropped out, a scrinatege being formed in cent-e, out Bate getting hold, passed to Belshaw. who, on being tackled by Lamble, trans- ferred the ball to Nevins. This player kicked; and follow. lag upe gained a try,. Boardman this time. falliog to im. Prove the point. Hilton kicked off, Adamson making a good return. Bate next passed to Belishave, whO made a capital drop at goal, the wind taking the ball just outside the pests, a dead ball resulting. After the dropout, Jones' Unsworth Yackett. and Eyes rushed the bell over the line, but Hilton succeeded in touching down. Immediately afterwards Boardman took a shot at goal, but failed. Unsworth also got over. but the ball well ruled dead, owing to it having touched the spectators. Time was called, and the score stood: Warrington one goal one try and twelve minor points to Edge Hill nil. Team's :Warrington—Full back, Jolley; three-quarter backs.Nevine, Belshaw, Board man (captain); half backs. Antrobits and pate; forwards, Adamson, E. Dil- lon, Molyneux. Jones,- Ashurst, Uasworth, Thornley, Eyes, and Hackett. Edge Hill—Full back, J. A. Hilton ; three- quarter becks, T. Williams, W. Hilton, and A.. E. ramble ;- halt backs. Middleton mid Barnes ; forwards, Morley, Bicker- ton, Tindley. Brandwood, Blackburn, W. Lamble, &rattle, McGrachin„ and Ellison. RUNCORN Y. NEN,/ Bansavox.—As usual on the Runcorn ground, there was a capital attendance to witeess Saturday's ' fixture, New Brighton meeting the town club. The day was beautifully fine and the going all that could be wished, and thone alto anticipated a fast game were not disap- pointed, for it was really a cracker from start to finish. From the very commencement the home players bad the foot of their opponents, who were beaten pointless by two goals, six tries, end four minors th nothing. This tall score would almost indicate an uninteresting game, but this was not so. as on occasions New Brighton played up capi- tally, and, indeed, never slackened their exertions to the last, but it was the tine combination of Roncorn, associated with perfect training, that upset them. R. Barber (three- quarters) and Q. Leitch (half) were the best of the New Brighton backs, the former running and kicking very well, whilst the latter tackled fearlessly. Amongst the forwards A. Williams, Blunt, and Gifford were best. The wieners played well to a man, both backs and forwards. Speakman and T Davies at three-quarters were brilliant, and the two half backs were not a whit less so. It was four o'clock sharp wben Rome kicked off for New Brighton. Woods returned, and Leitch mulled the ball, but pulling himself up smartly, together with R Woodwerd, invaded the Runcorn 25, and a scrimmage was formed within several yards of the goal line Clarke and Faulkner coming through to the centre, where Barber ran across without making much ground, and the ball was taken on the loose to the New Brighton end, where H Hughes passed to Speakinen, who took a drop and a dead ball reaulted. Instal:ale, following the drop-out W Hughes picked up and, forced his way in, and Broady notched a goal. Roma restarted and Speakman returned, and Barber, going at his best pace, was tickled by Wain- wright when looking dangerous. The New Brighton captain shortly after kicked to good purpose, and Leitch followed up, and was not arrested wail he had taken the ball over the quarter-line. The Runcorn forwards rallied, and corning along on the loose the centre mark was passed, and An- drews threw to Wainwright, who cored the goal line, Broady's place kick failing. Pretty passing by Andrews, Speakmen, and Davies resulted in a saving clause, and the same trio induced a second valueless point, and after Wil- liams had put in a useful run for the visitors half time was called. On turning about W Hughes set the ball going., and Barber replied, and Wainwriebt returntd, a scrimmage being finmed at the New Brighton 25 line, and Speakman passed to Davies, who ran behind, and Broady missed the goal from a bad position, and a similar fate betel a try ob, tamed by Lewis. New Brighton were kept en the line for a while, Male giving very temporary relief, and another Pass by Speakman to Davies ended in the latter getting in, but ' Broady again went wide of the poste. Speakman, going full' tilt, was brought up grandly by Leitch. Male dropped finely into touch, posted the centre line, but Speakman and Woods got down quickly, but Barber ran again into neutral ground and threw to Jones. Speakman was busy once more, and gave Davies a chance which nearly% came off, as he was tackled close to the line, but immediately H Hughes handed to Speakmaa. and be dropped over, and Broady placed a goal. A punt b.v W Riley caused New Brighton to touch down. No sooner was the ball dropped out than it was down again, and in a .scramble It wee kicked over the visitor? line, and Wainwright secured a try. Broady, however, did not improve it. A most artistic bit of passing between Davies, Riley, H Hughes, and Speakman ended. in the latter adding another try. Broady sent it over the bar, but, beimc fouled in treeleit, the higher point was not regis- tered. Tbis brought a one-sided, though pleasant, game to a close. Teams :—Runcorn T Woods, back; H C Speak- man, T Davies, and W Riley, three-quarter backs; H Hughes and H G Andrews, half backs; WII Broady, W Wright, W Hughes, W Faalkner, J Lewis, J Clarke, J Barnes, Or Wainwright, and J CiatleO. forwards. New Brighton: R Woodward, back; R Barber, W Rome, and W H Male. three•quarter backs ; Q T Leitch and C Wood- ward, half backs ; A Williams, J G Clifford, F W Jones, W Dutton, C Manifold„'R F Muir, K " Walker," H P Blunt, and B J Browne forwards.

div.p: WARRINGTON V. MANCHESTER FREE WANDERERS.

A fine match was witnessed on Saturday berws,rn the abovemamed teams on the Warrington ground. This being the last match on the Warrington list before entering on the cup ties, great interest was taken in it as an indication of the " form " of the cupbelders, and consequently over 3,000 spectators were present to witness the contest. Of their ordinary first team Warringtoa were short et Jolley Davies, and Rigby. Frank Turner kicked off, and his brother collared Ander- ton before he could return. div.head: WARRINGTON MUSEUM FREE LECTURES.
div.p: WARRINGTON MUSEUM FREE LECTURES.

- - - On Monday evening, the fifth of the series of free lectures at the Museum was given by Mr. T. Norris; subject, "The influence of machinery on the pros- perity of the people." There was again a good attend- ance. In the course of his paper, Mr. Morris said he found the word prosperity in the Imperial and other dictionaries to mean "Advance or gain in anything good or desirable; successful progress in any business or enterprise; as, , the prosperity of arts or sciences, agricultural or commercial pros- perity, national or individual blessings, comforts, accumulation of wealth, Sic." He could well re- member the time when machinery for agricultural purposes 'was thought to be a most uncalled for in- vention, and altogether antagonistic to the above sentence. For " puffing billy" to breathe the pure country atmospheric air instead of the farm and field labourer seemed somewhat preposterous. Re- ferring to the temporary evils that exist when I machinery is first introduced, Mr. Morris said it as about the year 1856 when the boot manufacturers lof Northampton and Stafford came to the conclusion to adopt the sewing machine, upon which the work people struck work. But no better method than t hat could have been adopted to drive their staple I trade from their own town to another, and to give the very bread their children should eat to others. I In this case, as in many like it, the need of machin- ery was felt, and the people could not be kept wait- ing for better and cheaper goods by any class of workpeople. Machinery had, must, and ever would gain the mastery over manual labour. To strike against it availeth not; it was simply making what people thought an eviLan actual one. Regarding the same machine quite the contrary action was taken by the boot and shoe operatives of Lynn, a town in the State id Massachusetts. When it was put before them they immediately adapted themselves to it, and by so doing kept their staple trade in their own town, and such was the increase in the populatiOn of shoemakers that in a short time proof showed itself that in one generation the number of shoemakers would increase 300 per cent. NoF for another instance. Many of them, as well as him- self, would well remember the time when the cloth, carpet, cotton, and other like machinery was introduced, scattering, as it did, the old hand loom weavers by the hundreds over the land. The evil here, if it could be called so, was in the rapid bring- ing forward of such like labour-saving machinery. These two instances would tend to show where the evil rested. In the first case it was brought on by the operatives themselves; in the latter the opera- tives were pushed out by an• invention that pro- duced by another method and increased the produc- tion by fifty and a, hundred fold. Thus they found that wherever that class of machinery came into operation it brought an evil upon a certain class for a time, but in all cases, a more or less great benefit on the existing and rising generation; therefore of ; all evils the least dust be chosen. When they did I this they would find that the evils were small lin comparison to the good, machinery being com- mended by all sterling, thinking men. In fact the ; good attending was as much to the benefit of the injured few as it was for the ma- jority, they being obliged by the call of nature to make use of those articles which the it machine produced to a greater and better advan- ; tage. But not only so, for so much more finished r goods were thrown into our markets that the value I of them was reduced, and the public, aye, some of I the poorest, have those goods as a common commo- dity which a few months previous they had not the remotest idea would ever fall to their share. (Ap- plause.) Before the days of mechanics life was not worth living. It was one of slavery and supersti- tion. Comforts were not known as we know them now. For many ages of the world's history the minds were few that could even investigate abstract truths, and when they did they did not know how to apply them. The sovereigns of Egypt, we read, had an enormcus amount of human labour at their comniand. and we cannot conceive the pain and toil their slaves endured while erecting the pyramids and other immense piles, simply to gratify their miserable minds while living and to contain their bones when dead. (Hear, hear.) The lecturer then referred in an interesting manner to the machinery of antiquity, and alluded to the great uses to which machinery had been put at different periods. At the conclusion of the paper it was announced that on Monday next the Rev. J. Yonge would give the I concluding lecture; subjeat, "Working-class Eng- land; fifty years ago and now."

div.p: WARRINGTON AND TUE QUEEN'S
JUBILEE.
Xetters to the Ottitor.
- - - - - - DEM/FY-MAYOR -" TO BE OR NOT TO ? "

'• Sir,—As a ratepayer of Warrington, who attended' the last Louncil meeting, / am curious to know who is Deputy- Mayor? saw that Alderman Harrison occupied the chair , which is supposed to be atlotted to the Mayor's deputy, but as he is not, and has no right toi be congidered the official in question, I must say that in my opinion it was hardly the thing to sit where be did. It we are to have a Deputy Mayor, let him be appointed at once, and for goodness sake don't let us have Alderman Harrison, or it it is not consi- dered desirable or necessary to appoint a deputy, let that be understood, and then we shall know who's who.—Yours, &c.
BOXER.

_ MR. CHAMBERLAIN ON THE LAND QUESTION. Sir,-1 have often wondered what class of politicians It could be who pester our publ,c men for opinions on the re- marks of others, and under what circumstances they are in- duced to renly. It is a pitiful case when you see a public man like Mr. Chamberlain reply in the manner he has done off the bare statement of a man that is nowhere except on his own cottage floor. Sir, the facts of the case are in a nutshell. My loquacious friend, Mr. Sutcliffe' interrupts Mr. Hewes; but when the time comes he will not mount the platform and contest a single sentence uttered by Mr. Howes, but quietly stabs him in the back by writing to Mr. Chamberlain. Well, sir, we all know that the Radical Cham- berlain has said nothing; but the Tory Chamberlain might have uttered something prompted by the jealousy of the other when the twins have been discussing the Augas: speech of 1895. It is the speeches of these Siamese twins that are caueing the derangement of a good many political minds, and should my Unionist friend receive his promised cow I shudder for the consequences, for at this time I defy anyone who has listened to him for five minutes to say whether he is for or against the motion he is speaking upon. It is painful to see a once good Radical led into the condition of mind I have pictured as political derange- mt, but it is so.—Yoars truly, JAMES TAYLOR. 48, Birchall-street, Warrineton, March 3rd, 1887.

some thousands of pounds. Where it it coming from? At I the meeting on Monday evening two fifty pound notes were promised. The promoters of the Library scheme are told they can have what they want as soon as they find a cheque Well, I suppose the same answer must be given to the play- ground promoters. So far as that goes, the two parties are in similar positions. There is a difference which you, sir, have more than once put to the front, that is, that there is a way of carrying out the Free Lending Library scheme, but it needs the Library Committee to find the will. Now, sir, the position I take is this. Nothing whatever will be done if every rich man buttons up his pocket; but if all the talk of loyalty we hear tell of is something more than smoke, then we shall see a fund formed, and the ques- tion will come how to wisely spend it? Now the Free Lending Library Committee my that their scheme is the best, as it will be an everlasting monument of the wisdom and foresight of the men of thia generation. 'I hey say k will meet one of the exigencies of the day; none but a Colonel will deny this. And, in conclusion, I may nay that they urge that their motives ars disinterested, inas- i much as each one of the leaders in the movement is already lin possession of a good library, and knows ire benefits. Those who oppose the idea cannot be real book lovers. JIM TODD.

div.head: TEAR'S LLBOURS.
div.p: A TEAR'S LLBOURS.

Mr. W. HANDLEY, the secretary, read a report, in which he reviewed the political work of the division during the past year. Having referred to the Liberal meetings that bad been held since the election, the report went on to Say :—" Frequent op- portunity has been afforded for discussion by the local Liberal clubs, which have been either resuscitated or called into existence as the result of our temporary defeat giving excellent nromise of political activity and healthy progress. It is a moot question whether the Divisional Associatiation workld not be acting wisely in taking these local clubs under its care, and becoming responsible for such part of the expenditure as cannot reasonably be expected to be met by merely local effort. The Association would receive in return centres for bolding district meetings, and a ready means of communisation with the Liberalism of the Division. The registration work was entrusted to the following local agents :—Mr. P. Watson, North wich, Marston, Davenham, and Barnion districts ; Mr. Tol- free, Over and Wharton; Mr. Williams, Middlewich ; Mr. Davidson, Weaverham and Aston ; your secre- tary, Runcorn North and South, and Halton; upon the secretary also devolved the general supervision, and the attendance at the reviaion courts through the division. The result was a net gain to the register of 291 voters, the majority of whom, we have every rea- son to believe, will vole Liberal at the next election. Of the finances of the Association our treasurer will report, but it may be remarked that while up to the present tile • funds have been subscribed by a comparatively few persons, it should be a matter of little moment to obtain the moderate amount required for the work of onr organ- isation seeing that we have a council of 360 and a voting power of 5,000. a nerainal subscription from each of whom would meet all demands." The report concluded with a "high tribute to Mr. Gladstone, as leader of the Liberal party. (Applause.)

Mr. A. PLETCUER moved. that Mr. E. 11. Moss. of Middlewich, be requPsted to retain the presidency for another year. Mr. Moss was surrounded by tempta- tions to go elsewhere—(l Jughter)—but he stuck true to his Lineralistn and true to his Nonconformity, and such a man was to be valued and made much f (Applause.) Mr, MILLINGTON, of *Middlewicb, seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously by acclamk tion. _

It was suggested by Mr. T. HANDLEY that Mr. Shaw should he the Chairmait of the Council, but that gentleman asked Co be excused on the plea that he had nat the time to devote to the office. The Rev. J. D. Trromes said unless Ur. TShaw absolutely refused he should propose that be be the Chairman of the Council. They all knew how hard he had worked for the Liberal chase in Cheshire, and those of them who lived in Runcorn knew that he was the backbone of Liberalism in the town. (Ap- plause.) JEPsort seconded the motion heartily, and it was carried by loud acclamation. The House Committee, in their minutes, recommended the Board to remit certain final which h,id been imposed upon the contractor for milk, Mr. Lowcock, in consequence of some of it not being of the quality stated in the agree- ment—Mr. James Burchall thought there bad been some irregularity about the contract. The milk was to be de. I Evered night and roornieg, but he believed that had not been adhered to, and the milk WAS not of that increasing quality as stated in the agreement. He thought the Guar- dians should not remit the fines, and he moved a resolution to that effect.—Mr. P. Longton seconded.—Mr. William. Middleburg did not believe the milk was genuine, and ift milk was supplied it should be genuine milk He ehould support the resolution.—Rev. Dean FinegAn did not believe at all in the principle of remitting fines. They should make contractors keep to their agreements—Mr. Jackson said after seeing the satisfactory manner n which the comrac- tor had fulfilled his duties, and considering that he had only three days' notice to commence to mop- ply, be thought the recommendation of the Howe Com. mittee should be adopted and the fines remittA. In those three days Mr. Lowcock could not get a sufficient supply except by giving up his customers, but be struggl,d to do the best he could to supply the house. It was during that time in the first month that the hulk of the lines were incurred, and it was reasonable they should be reinit,ed. The tobaggan business is only a [temporary mania. We'll bet a new hat that every slide in the country will be abandoned before July Ist. - ARGUMENT FOR MARRIAGE WITH A DECEASED WIFE'S SISTEIL—A man would thus be enabled to avoid having more than one mother-in-law. THE ROAD TO WEALTH.—A Harrisburg man has started, for free distribution, a religious journal called the Plumbline. If his object had, been to inake money, he would have called, it the Plumber. IT was NEW TO HIM.—" When you have the leisure," said a caller to the Snake Editor," I would like to speak to you." "Leisure !" replied the Snake Editor," what is that ?" A witness, giving evidence in a bicycle case, stated this as the result of his observations: "If you ride slow, you turn over yourself; if you ride fast, you turn over somebody else." Miss Younglove : "Here is a telegram I want sent at once, please." Operator: "Yes, miss?) Proceeds to count the words. Miss Younglove : "Stop, sir! How dare you read it. That message is confidential." HENRY'S LITTLE ERROR.—Flenry George says that an income tax is a tax on" conscience." We beg to asSure Mr. George that a tax on conscience wouldn't raise enough to feed a pointer dog. The Alta-California charges a Michigan woman with having kicked a bear to death. An investigation shows that she simply kicked her husband into an unconscious condition. Why not get these things right? There are no less than seventeen persons who claim to be "the silver-tongued orator of New England." It does one good to discover that modesty still exists among the old Puritan States. At a pioneers' meeting recently held in Wisconsin not a single lie was told, although 120 old pioneers were present and gave their experiences. It must have been an infernally dull old assemblage. The story that Western grasshoppers were being sold in the market for French sardines had no foundation in fact. All our French sardines are caught on the New England coast, and anything smaller than a shark is supposed to be a sardine. A woman at Columbus, 0., who went shopping the other day about a mile from home got so homesick that she cried and had to be sent off in a carriage before she had made a single purchase. There is no use in hoping that it will become epidemic. American railway-conductor: "Is there a total ab- stainer in this car ? " Passenger, promptly : "Yes, I'm one." Conductor, coming forward and speaking confi- dentially Let me take your pocket-pistol a minute, will you? There's a lady fainted over in the next car." "Did you pick up in weight by going to the seaside last year, Smithley ? " "I did, indeed, Brownley— gained one hundred and twenty-five pounds." "Pshaw ! Impossible!" "Fact, my dear fellow, Come up to the hottse,, and ru introduce you to her. We were married last month." Ground corn-stalks and prairie grass are mixed with a little coal, pressed into cakes a foot square and used in the prairie country with such satisfaction that the woman who discovered the process will soon be rich. A farmer who has business on the hay mow and doesn't leave a pitchfork where he can strike it as he descends is too absent-minded for any good, or else too mean to want to see the local newspapers get along and prosper. , -There is a church in Olney, 111., without a hypocrite In it. The other Sunday the clergyman invited the hypocrites to stand up and show themselves, and not a single person arose. The pastor must have been greatly il 02ns WAY TO Oar I.—ln a prohibition town in Maine some visitors went into a store kept by a German woman, and e.allerr for whiskey. She said she could not sell any, and then whispered to one of them, "en you vents fiskey, you must call for vine, and pinch mit von eye." ' Two young men at Shelbyville, Ind., fought thirty-five rounds to see who should marry a certain young lady. When the battle had been decided and the ambulance sent for it was learned that the girl had been married for a week to a chap who'd sooner run than fight. A San Francisco reporter who wrote up an interview with a silver king didn't tell one single lie from first to last, nor did he speak of the man's charming wife "or "elegant and refined residence." He was not, there- fore, greatly surprised next day to receive a check for SlO,OOO. "Yes, only two, hut the citizens are hopeful."

CARTER remarked that the ladies were stirring themselves in political matters, and it was beginning to be felt that the ladies were a power that ought to be taken advantage of. Could not the council do something to organise the ladies willing to act in the district.. Mr. Firm= replied that the matter would be considered at a future period. PLACE or NEXT MEETING. It was decided that the next annual meeting should be held at Winsford, and the next Council meeting within the year at Middlewich.

_ - The Queen left London at five o'clock on Friday afrnmoon by special train for Windsor. , It is now confidently stated that-the round table confer- ence is likely to result in an agraement as to the bas:a of settlement of the Irish question. From Paris it is telegraphed that the peaceful speech of the Emperor of Germany at the opeeing of the Reichstag has created an excellent impression. On Friday morning Robert Houghton' farm labourer, of Woodplumpton, near Preston, was found drowned in the limekiln basin of the Preston and Lancaster Canal. . Replying, on,Fridity, to a deputation which waited upon him to urge alterations in the system of collecting tithes, Lord Salisbury said the Government had prepared a bill on the subject. . Pulse Frown—Dave Burke and Dido f3opwood fought at Ealing on Friday morning. Twenty-fiva rounds were fought in 50 minutes, the result being a draw. It was the best contest ever seen, and was undisturbed. The police appeared t io late to interfere. Tan GOVERNMENT MEASURES FOR IRELAND,--The Ex- change Telegraph Company learns that Lord idertiegton has received all the details of the Irish policy of the Govern- ment, that he bas expressed his approval of the proposed measures, and promised his support. Among the more im- portant provisions of the Bill to Amend the Crim'inal. Law will be one giving the police power to arrest any person advocating illegal combinations. _ THE RISING IN BULGARIA. PARIS, PRIDAV.—A telegram received here irons Giur- gevo, of to-day's date states that risings have occurred at Tirnova and other places, and that the insurgents are masters of Tirnova. It is added that telegraphic commu- nication between Sofia and the provinces is interrupted. RENEWED EARTHQUAKE SHOCKS. A "Daily News" telegram from Naples says :—A• strong earthquake shock is reported from Reggio, Calabria'. A alight ehock was also felt along the Riviera. Nice, FRIDAY.—There was a slight earthquake chock here at five o'clock this morning. Some alarm WAi occa- sioned, but no damage was done. LOSS OF A SIEAMSHIP.—GALLANT RESCUE OF 118 PASSENGERS. The correspondent of the Central News at Vigo,,writing on the let inst., reports the loss of the Pacific Steam Navi- gation Company's steamer Talparasia, on the previous night, about a quarter-past ten o'clock. Most fortunately the Chanael Squadron was at author in the harbour, when the vessel struck on a rock about three miles off he passengers, one hundred and eighteen, mostly steerage, were in a state of panic. Most ottlaem were French and Spanish, and there was a large proportion of women. The whole of the passengers were saved, and taken on board the flagship. LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS. The House met at four o'clock. Lord FLU:GERALD drew attention to the administration of jury lams in Ireland, and denied that Roman Catholics were excluded from the jury panel in recent trials in Dublin on accoant of religion.—The Law of Evidence Amendment • Bill and Irish Solicitors' Bill were read a third time and nosed. The House then adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS. The House met at 4 o'clock. THE VACCINATION LAWS.—Mr-lincHlE, replying to Sir C. Russell, said the Government declined to institute aey inquiry into the working of the Vaccination Acts. THE COERCION 81LL..-Mr. W. H. SMITH, replying to Mr. E. Robertson, s.id the Government intended later In the season to move for a Select Committee to consider the question of grants to tha Royal family.—Replving to Mr. T. Healy, Mr. SMITE said with regard to the Irieh measure of the Government he had to say that as soon as the debate on procedure was brought to a close the Government would at once frankly and boldly state the nature of the proposals they inteeded to propose as re- gards Ireland. Tits PROCEDURE DEBATE.—The adjourned debate on Mr. Whitbread's amendment to provide that the initiative I closure should be by the Government, and not by the con- sent of the Speaker. was resumed.—Mr. W. SMITH opposed the amendment. The proposition had been given fair anct candid consideration, and the remit arrived at was that it would be unwise to omit the words which made it necessary that the consent of the chairman should be had before the closure was appl led.—Mr. OLAD3TONE had hoped that the Government would have accepted the ameedment. He thought there was now enough reeponsibility on the chair. —Lord AWN MANNERS defended the retention of the words. —The debate was continued by Mr. Courtney, Mr. T. P. O'Connor, Mr. Molloy, and other members, and Mr. Whit- bread's amendment was ultimately rejected by 177 to 129. [LEFT sirrrneo.
